#675. A 2,700-year-old solar eclipse just revealed something surprising about Earth

An international research team has revisited one of the oldest precisely dated records of a total solar eclipse, uncovering new details about how Earth's rotation has changed over thousands of years. By combining historical geography with modern astronomical calculations, the scientists reconstructed an eclipse that occurred in 709 BCE and determined how it would have appeared from Qufu, the ancient capital of China's Lu Duchy.

The researchers also examined an early account that may describe the solar corona, the Sun's faint outer atmosphere that becomes visible to the naked eye during a total solar eclipse. Their analysis of its possible shape suggests that the Sun was returning to a more active phase following an extended period of unusually low activity.

Published in Astrophysical Journal Letters, the findings provide more precise evidence of Earth's rotation speed in ancient times. They also offer potential independent support for previous reconstructions of solar activity based on radiocarbon measurements.

An Ancient Chinese Eclipse Record Holds a Crucial Clue

On July 17, 709 BCE, observers at the court of the Lu Duchy witnessed a total solar eclipse. The event was preserved in the "Spring and Autumn Annals," a historical chronicle compiled approximately 200 to 300 years later. The original account stated that "the Sun was totally eclipsed."

An additional description appears in the "Hanshu" (Book of Han), which preserves a passage written about seven centuries after the eclipse. This later account contains an unusual observation that may refer to the Sun's corona.

"What makes this record special isn't just its age, but also a later addendum in the 'Hanshu' (Book of Han) based on a quote written seven centuries after the eclipse. It describes the eclipsed Sun as 'completely yellow above and below.' This addendum has been traditionally associated with a record of a solar corona. If this is truly the case, it represents one of the earliest surviving written descriptions of the solar corona," explained lead author Hisashi Hayakawa, an assistant professor at Nagoya University's Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research and Institute for Advanced Research.

Initially, however, the historical account appeared to conflict with modern astronomy. When the team calculated the eclipse's path using existing estimates of Earth's ancient rotation, their results indicated that a total eclipse should not have been visible from the previously assumed location of the Lu court in Qufu.

The researchers traced the discrepancy to a mistake in the city's geographic coordinates. By examining archaeological excavation reports and historical geographic evidence, they determined that earlier calculations had placed ancient Qufu approximately eight kilometers from its actual location.

Correcting this relatively small error made it possible to reconstruct the eclipse more accurately and extract valuable information about Earth's rotation and the Sun's appearance.

"This correction allowed us to accurately measure the Earth's rotation during the total eclipse, calculate the orientation of the Sun's rotation axis, and simulate the corona's appearance," explained Hayakawa, who holds doctorates in solar physics and oriental history.

Why Ancient China Preserved Such Detailed Astronomical Records

The survival of this remarkable observation reflects the importance of astronomy in ancient Chinese society. Successive dynasties employed specialists to monitor celestial events because unusual phenomena in the sky were often interpreted as omens.

This practice, known as omenology, was closely connected to political beliefs. Eclipses, auroras, and other extraordinary astronomical events were sometimes considered warnings that an emperor had acted improperly.

As a result, court astronomers carefully documented changes in the sky. The records maintained across successive dynasties eventually became some of the world's most valuable historical sources for studying ancient eclipses.

Even so, the researchers emphasize an important distinction between the original eclipse observation and the later description of the corona.

The 709 BCE event is regarded as the earliest explicit written record of a total solar eclipse that can be securely dated. It may also be associated with one of the oldest surviving descriptions of the solar corona, but that interpretation remains uncertain because the relevant passage appears in a source written centuries after the event.

Although the corona account requires caution, the established timing of the eclipse provides a reliable basis for investigating Earth's historical rotation. The possible corona description also offers a valuable comparison with other studies of ancient solar activity.

How a 2,700-Year-Old Eclipse Reveals Earth's Faster Rotation

Earth does not rotate at a perfectly constant rate. Over long periods, its spin has gradually slowed, partly because of friction associated with ocean tides generated by the Moon's gravitational pull.

Consequently, Earth rotated slightly faster 2,700 years ago than it does today.

Using the revised position of ancient Qufu, the researchers obtained improved constraints on Earth's rotation during the period spanning the eighth through sixth centuries BCE.

Their calculations placed delta T (ΔT), a measurement used to describe variations in Earth's rotation relative to a uniform time scale, between 20,264 and 21,204 seconds for the eclipse of 709 BCE.

"This new dataset fixes coordinate errors in previous Earth rotation studies. Additionally, it improves the accuracy of dating and reconstructing historical astronomical events," said coauthor Mitsuru Sôma of the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan.

These measurements help scientists better understand changes in the length of Earth's day over thousands of years. They can also improve calculations of when and where other ancient astronomical events would have been visible.

Evidence That the Sun Was Awakening From a Long Quiet Period

Beyond revealing Earth's rotational history, the eclipse may provide evidence of an important transition in the Sun's activity.

Scientists have previously reconstructed ancient solar cycles by studying radiocarbon preserved in tree rings. The possible corona description from 709 BCE offers another way to examine those findings.

"This unique historical addendum for the possible solar coronal structure is critical for providing a spot reference on solar activity reconstructions from tree rings and ice cores, as well as providing independent validation of solar activity models," explained coauthor Mathew Owens, a professor of space physics at the University of Reading.

Trees absorb carbon from the atmosphere during photosynthesis, including small amounts of radioactive carbon known as radiocarbon. Some of this material becomes locked into annual growth rings, creating a natural record that researchers can examine thousands of years later.

Radiocarbon levels are influenced by cosmic rays reaching Earth's atmosphere. When the Sun becomes more active, its magnetic influence generally reduces the number of cosmic rays that reach Earth, affecting radiocarbon production.

By measuring changes in radiocarbon concentrations across successive tree rings, scientists can reconstruct how solar activity varied long before modern instruments existed.

The Sun normally follows an activity cycle lasting approximately 11 years, during which the number of sunspots and the strength of solar magnetic activity rise and fall.

Occasionally, however, the Sun enters much longer periods of reduced activity called "grand minima." During these intervals, sunspots become exceptionally rare, and the usual cycle is much less pronounced.

One such interval, known as the "Neo Assyrian Grand Minimum" or "Homer Grand Minimum," lasted from approximately 808 to 717 BCE.

The eclipse of 709 BCE took place shortly after this prolonged quiet period ended.

According to the researchers, the possible description of the solar corona is consistent with a Sun that had resumed its regular activity cycles. Its apparent structure suggests substantial magnetic activity and indicates that the Sun may have been near the peak of its approximately 11-year cycle at the time.

This interpretation agrees with earlier solar activity reconstructions derived from radiocarbon measurements in tree rings, although the uncertainty surrounding the historical corona description means it cannot be considered definitive proof.

Ancient Astronomers Are Still Helping Scientists Understand the Universe

The findings demonstrate how observations preserved for thousands of years can continue to contribute to modern scientific discoveries.

By bringing together historical documents, archaeological evidence, geographic research, and sophisticated astronomical models, scientists can recover information that would otherwise be impossible to measure directly.

In this case, a correction of just eight kilometers helped transform an ancient eclipse record into a more precise source of information about Earth's rotation and a potential window into the Sun's distant past.

"Some of our ancestors were very skilled observers," noted coauthor Dr. Meng Jin of the Lockheed Martin Solar and Astrophysics Laboratory. "When we combine their careful records with modern computational methods and historical evidence, we can potentially find new information about our planet and our star from thousands of years ago."

Gaspra was the first asteroid to ever be visited by a spacecraft.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Oct. 29, 1991, the Galileo spacecraft flew by the asteroid Gaspra on its way to Jupiter. Gaspra was the first asteroid to ever be visited by a spacecraft.

Gaspra orbits near the inner edge of the asteroid belt. The Galileo spacecraft had been travelling through the asteroid belt for about two months before it reached Gaspra. Galileo was 990 miles (1,593 kilometers) away from Gaspra when it whizzed by, and it was travelling at a relative speed of about 5 miles (8 km) per second.

The spacecraft took several photos of the asteroid and used an instrument called the Near-Infrared Mapping Spectrometer to study its chemical composition and other physical properties. Galileo determined that Gaspra has an irregular and elongated shape measuring about 12 miles long and 7 miles wide. The images revealed that Gaspra was also covered in craters. Because Galileo was too far away for Gaspra's gravity to affect it, the spacecraft was not able to determine the asteroid's mass.

The Galileo spacecraft's flyby of Gaspra was a pitstop near the midpoint of its 6-year journey to Jupiter, the largest planet in our solar system. NASA launched Galileo toward Jupiter in October 1989, with the probe swinging by Venus and Earth in 1990 before its encounter with Gaspra.

The Gaspra flyby was the first asteroid flyby in history, with Galileo approaching to just under 1,000 miles (1,601 kilometers) while flying at a whopping 18,000 mph. Galileo's photos of Gaspra "revealed a cratered, complex, irregular body about 20 by 12 by 11 kilometers (12.4 by 7.4 by 6.8 miles), with a thin covering of dust and rubble," NASA wrote in an overview.

"The picture we get of Gaspra is one of something that has suffered a lot during its history," the UPI press service quoted Joseph Veverka, a Galileo imaging team member, as saying at the time. "We suspect that this is the survivor of a series of catastrophic collisions in the past."

Galileo would go on to fly by Earth a second time in 1992, then swing close by the asteroid Ida in 1993 before finally arriving at Jupiter in 1995. Along the way, the probe was in the right place at the right time to watch as the Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 broke into pieces and crashed into Jupiter in July 1994.

Since Galileo's historic first asteroid flyby, NASA and other space agencies have gone on to land on asteroids (like NEAR on asteroid Eros), collect samples of asteroids and return them to Earth (like NASA's OSIRIS-REx and Japan's Hayabusa probes), and have even intentionally crashed probes into asteroids (like NASA's DART asteroid impact mission) to test planetary protection techniques.

#673. Stellantis stock rises 13% as automaker's turnaround plan, cost cuts gain traction

Shares of Stellantis were up Wednesday as the European car giant's third-quarter results showed it was making progress with its 60 billion euro turnaround plan.

Third-quarter revenues rose 1% to 37.6 billion euros from a year ago, the Chrysler and Jeep owner said on Wednesday, while adjusted operating income rose 184% to 256 million euros from 90 million euros a year earlier.

The automaker's industrial free cash flow improved to negative 4 billion euros, up from negative 4.3 billion the year prior.

Stellantis on Wednesday also reconfirmed its 2026 guidance and target to achieve positive free cash flow next year, which is a main focus for investors.

"Q3 was soft, but consensus expectations were far lower. Key here is that '26 Guidance was maintained while other auto OEMs and suppliers are cutting on elevated costs," RBC Capital Markets analyst Tom Narayan said Wednesday in an investor note.

Stellantis stock on the New York Stock Exchange rose 13% on Wednesday to close at $4.69 a share. Shares in Milan closed at 4.28 euros, up 15.4%. Shares in both markets remain sharply down since the beginning of the year.

Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa told investors Wednesday that the company is ahead of schedule on its turnaround plan, which was announced in May. He said Stellantis expects to exceed its previously announced cost-cutting efforts of 6 billion euros under the plan by 2028, including 2.4 billion euros to start 2027.

"We are very confident in reaffirming our '26 guidance. Those include '27 free cash flow positive," Filosa said Wednesday in response to concerns about the carmaker's ability to achieve its free cash flow target.

Stellantis' 2026 guidance includes a mid-single-digit percentage increase in net revenue and a low-single-digit adjusted operating margin.

Stellantis' turnaround plan includes investing 36 billion euros in its portfolio of automotive brands, with 60% of the cash to go towards its struggling North America sector. It also plans to introduce new vehicles, refresh models, and incorporate new technologies in its products.

Stellantis is targeting roughly 23% revenue growth, from 154 billion euros last year to 190 billion euros by 2030, with a 7% adjusted operating margin by then.

European carmakers, including Stellantis, have been struggling in China as domestic brands like Xiaomi, BYD and Geely gain ground and intensify competition.

Just this week, German luxury carmaker Porsche said it would reduce its exposure to China as car sales decline in the region. Meanwhile, Mercedes-Benz said its third-quarter car sales slumped due to a "challenging market environment," in the country.

Earlier this month, Filosa told CNBC that European regulators need to do more to incentivize carmakers to manufacture vehicles in the region to fend off Chinese rivals.

Filosa called for regulation that "incentivizes, rewards, and protects the ones that are able to demonstrate that they design cars, engineer cars."

#672. Scientists discover a surprising clue to why some brains resist Alzheimer’s

Some people have the brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease but never develop dementia. While others experience worsening memory and thinking problems, these individuals remain mentally sharp despite signs of the disease in their brains. Scientists have long struggled to explain why.

Now, researchers at the Netherlands Institute for Neuroscience have uncovered a promising clue. Their findings suggest that a rare group of brain cells, known as immature neurons, may behave differently in people who resist Alzheimer's symptoms. Rather than simply replacing damaged cells, these neurons could help protect the brain from the harmful effects of the disease.

This remarkable ability is known as cognitive resilience. It describes how some people maintain their memory and thinking abilities even when their brains show signs of damage or disease.

"Around 30 percent of older adults who develop Alzheimer's disease never experience its symptoms," says Evgenia Salta, senior author of the research. "We really don't know why. That's a big mystery, and a very important one."

Understanding this mystery could transform how scientists approach Alzheimer's, shifting attention from what causes brain cells to deteriorate toward what allows certain brains to remain healthy and functional.

One possible explanation for cognitive resilience is that some brains have a greater ability to repair or protect themselves as Alzheimer's progresses.

"Perhaps they can add new brain cells to a network that is degenerating," Salta says.

This possibility involves a biological process called adult neurogenesis, which refers to the production of new nerve cells (neurons) in an adult brain. Neurons are specialized cells that transmit information throughout the nervous system, allowing us to think, learn, remember, and respond to our surroundings.

Scientists have established that adult neurogenesis occurs in several animal species. Whether it continues to happen in the adult human brain, however, has been a subject of scientific debate for decades.

If the human brain can produce new neurons later in life, those cells might help maintain important connections as aging and disease damage existing networks. However, finding immature neurons does not necessarily prove that they were recently formed.

To investigate this possibility, Salta and her colleagues examined donated human brain tissue obtained through the Netherlands Brain Bank, a research resource that collects and preserves brain samples.

The researchers compared three groups: people without detectable brain pathology, patients who developed Alzheimer's dementia, and individuals whose brains showed Alzheimer's pathology but who remained cognitively resilient.

The team concentrated on a small region within the brain's memory center, an area believed to be among the few locations where new neurons might develop.

Finding the relevant cells was far from straightforward.

"These cells are extremely rare, so we had to develop new ways to find them," Salta says. "We really zoomed in on the exact spot where we expected them to be."

The researchers also developed new approaches to analyzing their data, allowing them to identify the cells more precisely without relying heavily on assumptions drawn from animal studies.

Scientists Find Immature Neurons in Brains Over 80

The search revealed something remarkable. Immature neurons were present across all three groups, including in the brains of older adults.

These cells resemble neurons that have not yet fully matured, suggesting that the aging brain may retain cellular features associated with development and adaptability.

"Even at an average age of over 80, we still found these immature neurons in all groups," Salta says.

But the most intriguing discovery came when researchers compared the brains of people who had developed dementia with those who had remained mentally sharp despite Alzheimer's pathology.

Initially, the scientists expected resilient individuals to have substantially more immature neurons. If these cells help replace damaged neurons, having greater numbers might explain why some brains withstand the disease.

Instead, the difference in cell numbers was much smaller than anticipated.

That unexpected result pointed toward another explanation. The important distinction might not be how many immature neurons a brain contains, but how those cells respond when the brain comes under attack.

A Hidden Defense Against Alzheimer's Damage

When the team examined the activity of immature neurons more closely, they identified striking differences between the groups.

In cognitively resilient individuals, the cells showed signs of activating biological processes associated with survival and protection against damage.

"In resilient individuals, these cells seem to activate programs that help them survive and cope with damage," Salta says. "We also see lower signals related to inflammation and cell death."

Inflammation is part of the body's normal defense system, but when it becomes persistent in the brain, it can contribute to damage and interfere with communication between neurons. Cell death, meanwhile, gradually disrupts the networks responsible for memory and thinking.

The findings suggest that immature neurons in resilient brains may be better equipped to withstand these harmful conditions.

More surprisingly, their role might extend beyond protecting themselves.

"It might not be (only) about replacing lost neurons," Salta explains. "It could be that these cells support the surrounding tissue and help the brain stay functional and 'youthful'. They may act as a sort of fertilizer in a garden that has started falling apart."

In other words, rather than serving only as replacements for dying neurons, immature cells could potentially help maintain the environment surrounding existing brain cells.

Such support might allow neural networks to continue functioning even as Alzheimer's related damage accumulates.

Why Scientists Are Cautious About the Discovery

Although the results offer an intriguing explanation for cognitive resilience, Salta emphasizes that the researchers have not established exactly what these immature neurons do.

Their conclusions about the cells' possible protective roles are based on patterns observed in brain tissue, not direct experiments demonstrating those functions.

"We assume the cells' function based on the data, but we cannot confirm it in this type of study," she explains.

That distinction is particularly important because research on adult neurogenesis has attracted considerable public attention, sometimes leading to claims that go beyond what scientists have demonstrated.

The presence of immature neurons does not establish that new neurons are continuously being produced in older humans, nor does it prove that these cells are responsible for preventing dementia.

Other biological mechanisms almost certainly contribute to cognitive resilience as well.

"This is one piece of a very large puzzle," Salta concludes. "There will never be just one factor that explains resilience."

Could Alzheimer's Research Shift Toward Protecting the Brain?

The findings raise a broader question about aging: Why do some people's brains remain relatively stable while others experience progressive cognitive decline?

"Somewhere along this trajectory, there's a kind of decision point," Salta explains. "Some people remain stable, others develop dementia. We want to understand what drives that difference."

To explore this further, the researchers plan to investigate how immature neurons communicate and interact with neighboring brain cells. Understanding those relationships may reveal whether the cells actively contribute to resilience and how their protective responses might work.

The research also reflects a growing change in how scientists think about Alzheimer's disease.

Traditionally, much of the field has focused on understanding the processes that damage the brain, including the accumulation of abnormal proteins and the loss of neurons. Increasingly, researchers are also asking why some brains remain functional despite those changes.

By identifying the mechanisms behind this natural resistance, scientists hope to uncover new ways to preserve memory and cognitive abilities as people age.

"Cognitive resilience is extremely exciting," Salta says. "If we understand what protects these brains, it could eventually lead to new therapeutic strategies."

Although practical treatments remain a distant possibility, the discovery suggests that even in old age, the human brain may possess protective abilities that scientists are only beginning to understand.

The distinguished British actor of stage and screen passed away Wednesday (Oct. 28) in Los Angeles.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Less than a week after the fates took Walter Koenig from our galaxy, another "Star Trek" legend has left us: Sir Patrick Stewart has died at the age of 86.

According to his spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak, the beloved Shakespearean actor passed away on Wednesday (Oct. 28) at his Los Angeles home after a short struggle with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.

"He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," Bush Novak shared. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace."

The first time I ever saw Patrick Stewart was in director John Boorman’s masterful 1981 King Arthur film, "Excalibur." As a young teenager, I was immediately captivated by his commanding presence and charisma portraying King Leodegrance of Cameliard — Queen Guinevere’s noble father and a cunning warrior.

In 1984, he entered the sci-fi realm in David Lynch's grand and ambitious adaptation of Frank Herbert's "Dune," in which he played Paul Atreides' good friend and mentor, War Master Gurney Halleck.

Stewart was later cast as the U.S.S. Enterprise’s Capt. Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation. He entranced millions of viewers in this role, traveling the final frontier with his gallant crew and redefining the brave and compassionate traits of a Federation starship commander. His adventurous journey on that popular show, a spinoff of "Star Trek: The Original Series," ran from 1987 to 1994, encompassing 178 episodes across seven seasons confronting Klingons, Cardassians, Romulans and The Borg.

When the series ended, Stewart continued on in the Enterprise's center seat by starring in four "Star Trek" feature films: 1994’s "Star Trek: Generations," 1996’s "Star Trek: First Contact," 1998’s "Star Trek: Insurrection," and 2002’s "Star Trek: Nemesis." Stewart also reprised the role of Jean-Luc Picard in three seasons of Paramount+’s "Star Trek: Picard," which ran from 2020 to 2023.

Stewart's prodigious talent was on further display in the hit adaptations of Marvel’s "The X-Men." He played the powerful, wheelchair-bound telepath Professor Charles Xavier in 2000’s "X-Men," 2003’s "X2: X-Men United," 2006’s "X-Men: The Last Stand," 2014’s "X-Men: Days of Future Past," and 2017’s "Logan."

Stewart, and Xavier, were prominently featured in those films. The actor and character also appeared in 2009’s "X-Men Origins: Wolverine" and 2013’s "The Wolverine," and will do so again in "Avengers: Doomsday," which will be released around Christmastime this year.

Aside from the two "Star Trek" and "The X-Men" franchise roles, Stewart had a flourishing career that spanned radio, stage and screen and was always a stellar attraction at any comic-con or other fan event around the world. Another of his many memorable projects was the compelling one-man stage show in which he played all the characters in Charles Dickens' novella "A Christmas Carol," captured on a two-disc CD set that I listen to each holiday season.

Knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010, Sir Patrick Stewart leaves behind a remarkable legacy that brought a rare gravitas and humanity to every performance he was ever involved in, and his passing leaves fans, friends and loved ones with heavy hearts. Here’s to a wonderful life well-lived!

#670. Exercise doesn't just strengthen your heart. It rewires it

Exercise does more than make the heart stronger. New research suggests it also physically reshapes the nerves that control the heart, revealing an unexpected difference between the left and right sides of the body.

Scientists at the University of Bristol (UK) discovered that moderate aerobic exercise changes the structure of nerve cells involved in regulating heart activity. Even more surprisingly, the changes were dramatically different on the two sides of the body. The findings, published in Autonomic Neuroscience, could eventually help doctors develop more precise treatments for irregular heartbeats, chest pain, angina, and stress-induced 'broken-heart' syndrome.

The discovery was made in rats, so further research is needed to determine whether the same changes occur in humans. Nevertheless, it offers a new perspective on how physical activity influences the nervous system that keeps the heart functioning.

Exercise Changes the Heart's Hidden Control System

The heart is regulated partly by the autonomic nervous system, a network of nerves that automatically manages essential functions such as heartbeat, breathing, and digestion. One branch of this system helps the heart beat faster when the body needs more oxygen, such as during exercise or stressful situations.

Small clusters of nerve cells called stellate ganglia play an important role in this process. Located on both sides of the lower neck and upper chest, these nerve hubs send signals that influence heart rate and other aspects of heart function.

The new research suggests that regular exercise changes these nerve clusters in ways scientists had not previously recognized.

Study lead author Dr. Augusto Coppi, Senior Lecturer in Veterinary Anatomy at the University of Bristol, said: "The discovery points to a previously hidden left-right pattern in the body's 'autopilot' system that helps run the heart.

"These nerve clusters act like the heart's dimmer switch and we've shown that regular, moderate exercise remodels that switch in a side-specific way. This could help explain why some treatments work better on one side than the other and, in future, help doctors target therapies more precisely and effectively."

Just 10 Weeks of Exercise Produced Striking Nerve Changes

To investigate how exercise affects these nerve clusters, the researchers examined rats that underwent 10 weeks of moderate aerobic training. Aerobic exercise is physical activity that increases heart rate and breathing, such as brisk walking, swimming, or cycling.

The study involved researchers from University College London (UCL) in the UK, the University of São Paulo (USP), and the Federal University of São Paulo (UNIFESP) in Brazil.

The team used advanced three-dimensional analysis techniques known as stereology to examine the nerve cells. This approach allows scientists to estimate the number, size, and distribution of cells within tissues.

The results revealed an unusual imbalance between the two sides of the body. In the trained rats, the cardiovascular nerve cluster on the right contained roughly four times as many neurons as the cluster on the left, a striking difference from the pattern observed in untrained rats.

The nerve cells also changed in size, but in opposite directions. Neurons on the left nearly doubled in size, while those on the right became slightly smaller.

These findings suggest that exercise does not affect all the nerves controlling the heart equally. Instead, it produces distinct structural changes on each side, potentially providing clues about how the nervous system adapts to regular physical activity.

Could the Discovery Lead to Better Heart Treatments?

The findings may have important implications for treating conditions involving abnormal nerve activity around the heart.

Arrhythmias occur when the heart beats too quickly, too slowly, or irregularly. Angina is chest pain or discomfort typically caused by insufficient blood flow to the heart muscle. Another condition, commonly called 'broken-heart' syndrome, involves a sudden weakening of the heart muscle that is often triggered by intense emotional or physical stress.

In some patients, doctors treat these problems by reducing excessive nerve signals reaching the heart. Procedures such as stellate ganglion nerve blocks temporarily interrupt nerve activity, while denervation involves disrupting certain nerve pathways.

Understanding how the left and right nerve clusters differ could eventually help physicians determine which side should be targeted for the greatest benefit.

Dr. Coppi explained: "Irregular heart rhythms, known as arrhythmias, stress-induced 'broken-heart' syndrome, and certain types of chest pain are often treated by dialing down overactive stellate ganglia -- the paired small nerve hubs in the lower neck/upper chest area that send 'go faster' signals to the heart.

"By mapping how exercise changes these ganglia on each side, the study offers clues that could one day fine-tune procedures like nerve blocks or denervation to the side most likely to help. The findings are early-stage and in rats, so clinical studies would need to follow."

What's Next for Exercise and Heart Research?

Although the structural changes were substantial, scientists still need to establish exactly how they affect heart function.

The research team plans to investigate whether the differences between the left and right nerve clusters influence how the heart behaves during rest and physical activity. They also intend to look for similar patterns in other animal models and eventually in humans.

For human studies, the researchers hope to use noninvasive markers, which could provide information about nerve activity without requiring surgery or tissue removal.

If the same left-right differences are found in people, the discovery could help guide more personalized treatments for arrhythmias, difficult-to-treat angina, and stress-induced 'broken-heart' syndrome.

Dr. Coppi added: "Understanding these left-right differences could help us personalize treatments for heart rhythm disorders and angina. Our next step is to test how these structural changes map onto function and whether similar patterns appear in larger animals and humans."

On the plus side, its year only lasts 11 hours!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth would be terrifying if we celebrated Halloween every 11 hours, a possibility on a super-Earth investigated by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). That is, if this extrasolar planet, or exoplanet, wasn't so hellishly hot that no life could survive on its surface.

The exoplanet in question is the rocky lava planet TOI-561 b, located around 280 light-years away, which was discovered by NASA's exoplanet-hunting spacecraft TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) in 2020. The planet is located so close to its star, TOI-561, that not only does it complete an orbit every 11 hours, but its surface temperatures reach in excess of 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit (1,800 degrees Celsius).That is so hot that astronomers once believed that TOI-561 b couldn't possibly possess an atmosphere. With 37 hours of JWST observations covering nearly four full orbits of TOI-561, scientists have now found this horrific planet is buried in a reflective layer of vaporized silicate mineral clouds, the same family of compounds that make up quartz and sand.

"We measured how the planet's brightness and heat changed throughout its orbit," team member Lisa Dang of the University of Waterloo said in a statement. "This technique, known as a phase curve, revealed that the planet reflects a significant amount of light from its star, and that heat is being redistributed around the planet instead of only on the sunlit side. Together, these point to the presence of an atmosphere."

The proximity of TOI-561 b to its star has another consequence. The planet is tidally locked, meaning it doesn't turn like Earth. Thus, TOI-561 b has one blisteringly hot "dayside" permanently facing its star, and a cooler "nightside" facing out into space in perpetuity.

Dang and colleagues investigated the fact that the bare rock of the dayside seemed to be cooler than should be expected. They theorized that missing heat could be carried around to the night side or the heat may be reflected away before TOI-561 b can absorb it.

By using the JWST to observe full orbits of TOI-561 b, the team was able to observe the planet's nightside for the first time. They found it isn't warm enough to account for all the heat missing from the dayside.

That means TOI-561 b must reflect roughly three-quarters of the starlight that hits it. That is comparable to the most reflective planet in the solar system, Venus, which reflects around 75% of incident sunlight compared to the 30% reflected by Earth.

The team determined that this high reflectivity is the result of clouds of silicate minerals, including silicon dioxide and magnesium silicate, forming on the planet's dayside and acting like sunscreen. These clouds could also help TOI-561 b hang on to an atmosphere.

Of course, the team can't yet be sure what this atmosphere is composed of. It could be a dense carbon dioxide fog like that seen on Venus, or it could be a blanket of sulfur dioxide like that of the most volcanic body in the solar system, Jupiter's moon Io. That would be the case if, like on Io, volcanic activity is replenishing the atmosphere of TOI-561 b.

"The next big question we will seek to answer is whether TOI-561 b's atmosphere resembles Venus or an extreme version of Io," Dang said. "Observing the planet at longer wavelengths with JWST could give us insights and help explain how a planet this hot has held on to an atmosphere for billions of years."The team's research was published in The Astronomical Journal.

He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. #668. Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue

Scientists at the University of Bonn have discovered that spiders experience distinct stages of sleep, including a REM-like state that shares surprising similarities with human sleep. During this stage, the spiders move their eyes and twitch their muscles, behaviors also associated with REM (rapid eye movement) sleep in humans and other vertebrates.

The findings provide the first comprehensive experimental confirmation that spiders experience genuine, regulated sleep rather than simply remaining inactive. They also raise intriguing questions about how sleep evolved and whether animals with very different nervous systems might share some of its fundamental features.

Researchers at the University of Bonn's Institute of Organismic Biology made the discovery while studying the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a small but remarkably sophisticated predator.

A Tiny Spider With Remarkable Hunting Skills

The Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata is only about the size of a one-euro coin when fully grown, but its hunting abilities make it particularly interesting to scientists.

Unlike many spiders that primarily capture insects, members of the genus Portia specialize in hunting other spiders. They use a variety of sophisticated strategies to catch their prey, including imitating the vibrations made by struggling insects trapped in spiderwebs.

These deceptive signals can lure web-building spiders toward what appears to be an easy meal, only for them to encounter the hunting Portia instead.

Such complex behaviors suggest that these spiders have unusual learning abilities, making them valuable subjects for investigating the relationship between sleep, nervous system function, and cognition.

Scientists Discover Two Distinct Stages of Spider Sleep

Although sleep has been extensively studied in humans and other vertebrates, scientists still know relatively little about how it works in animals with very different nervous systems.

To investigate whether spiders experience genuine sleep and whether that sleep includes different stages, the researchers closely monitored Portia fimbriata over several days and nights.

They discovered that the spiders exhibit two clearly distinguishable sleep stages. One of these resembles REM sleep, the phase in humans associated with rapid eye movements, muscle activity, and vivid dreaming.

During this REM-like stage, the spiders displayed characteristic eye movements and muscle twitches. These observations suggest that some features of sleep previously studied mainly in vertebrates may also occur in spiders.

The researchers emphasize that identifying REM-like movements does not establish whether spiders dream. However, the discovery provides important evidence that sleep in these animals is more complex than previously understood.

How Researchers Confirmed That Spiders Really Sleep

To study the spiders' sleeping behavior, the team placed individual Portia fimbriata spiders in plastic dishes measuring 12 centimeters in diameter. They monitored the animals under different lighting conditions to examine their daily activity and rest cycles.

Infrared cameras allowed the researchers to observe the spiders throughout the night without relying on visible light. Detailed recordings captured their sleeping positions, periods of quiet rest, and episodes of REM-like movement.

The team also conducted experiments to determine whether the spiders were genuinely asleep rather than simply sitting motionless.

Using sound stimuli, the researchers measured how quickly the spiders responded to disturbances. These tests helped distinguish sleep from ordinary inactivity.

Another important part of the investigation involved sleep deprivation. The researchers examined whether the spiders displayed "sleep rebound," meaning they compensated for interrupted sleep by increasing their subsequent sleep.

Together, the behavioral observations and experimental tests provided strong evidence that Portia fimbriata experiences regulated sleep with distinct stages.

Studying Spider Sleep Presented Unusual Challenges

Determining whether a spider is truly asleep is considerably more complicated than observing a sleeping human.

Because spiders sense their surroundings differently from people, the researchers first had to identify a sound stimulus that would produce a consistent response during their experiments.

They also needed to avoid assuming that the observed eye movements and muscle twitches necessarily represented the same processes seen during human REM sleep.

One major limitation was that the researchers could not measure the spiders' brain activity. Instead, they relied entirely on carefully documented behavior to identify different sleep states.

This required extensive high-resolution video recordings collected over many days and nights, producing enormous amounts of data for analysis.

Despite these obstacles, the combination of behavioral monitoring, response testing, and sleep disruption experiments allowed the researchers to build a detailed picture of how these spiders sleep.

What Spider Sleep Could Reveal About Evolution

The discovery has implications that extend well beyond spiders.

Most scientific knowledge about sleep comes from studying vertebrates, particularly mammals and birds. Finding comparable sleep features in animals with radically different nervous systems could help researchers understand when and why different types of sleep evolved.

The results also open new opportunities in behavioral science, neuroscience, and chronobiology, the study of biological rhythms.

By investigating sleep in a wider variety of animals, scientists hope to identify features that are shared across species and uncover the fundamental biological functions that sleep may have served early in evolutionary history.

The researchers argue that future investigations should move beyond traditionally studied animals and include species with unusual adaptations or much simpler nervous systems.

Such comparisons could reveal whether certain sleep mechanisms are widespread throughout the animal kingdom or developed independently in different evolutionary lineages.

Even after decades of intensive research, many basic questions about sleep remain unanswered, including important mysteries surrounding human sleep.

Could Spiders Dream? Scientists Have More Questions

The University of Bonn team is now expanding its research to investigate how sleep, particularly REM-like sleep, varies across different spider species.

Scientists are also comparing spiders sleeping in natural environments with those observed in laboratories to determine how surroundings influence their behavior.

Another major goal is to investigate the relationship between sleep and cognitive abilities. Researchers want to understand what happens inside the brains of spiders and insects during sleep, and whether different sleep stages contribute to learning and other mental processes.

Environmental changes are also becoming an important focus. The team plans to examine how climate change and human activities, especially artificial light at night (ALAN), may interfere with the sleep patterns of spiders and other arthropods.

For now, the findings establish that even a tiny jumping spider can experience a surprisingly complex form of sleep. Whether spiders actually dream remains unknown, but their nighttime behavior is offering scientists new clues about one of biology's most enduring mysteries.

Early risers across the U.S. could catch a glimpse of China's mysterious Shenlong spacecraft with the naked eye.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

China's secretive space plane is making a series of passes over the United States in the coming days and you could spot it with your own eyes!

The mysterious spacecraft, Shenlong, is currently orbiting Earth on its fourth mission. Although we don't know what it's up to, China's space agency has said it is testing technologies that "will pave the way for more convenient and affordable round-trip methods for the peaceful use of space in the future."

Under favorable conditions, Shenlong is bright enough to spot with the naked eye, according to Spaceweather.com. But you'll need to set your alarm early, as some of the best viewing opportunities are in the predawn sky.

According to satellite-tracking website Heavens-Above, skywatchers across the U.S. have several opportunities to spot Shenlong between Oct. 30 and early November, weather permitting.

Here are some of the most promising high-altitude passes for four major U.S. cities. All times are local, with the end of daylight saving time on Nov. 1 taken into account. Times are approximate and may change. Maximum elevation refers to the spacecraft's highest angle above the horizon, with 90° being directly overhead.

If clouds get in the way (or you forget to set your alarm), don't worry! There are several other opportunities over the coming days.

These predictions are specific to each city, so your exact viewing times will depend on your viewing location.

To find out when Shenlong will pass over your location, head to Heavens-Above, enter your location (in the top right corner of the page), then on the homepage look for "satellite database" under the satellites subheader. And search for "PRC TEST SPACECRAFT 4".

Select "visible only" to see upcoming passes and click on a date to bring up a detailed sky chart showing the spacecraft's predicted path across the sky, including where to look and when.

To the naked eye, Shenlong will look like a small, steadily moving point of light, similar to a satellite gliding across the sky.

Its brightness can vary significantly. Veteran satellite observer Paul Maley spotted Shenlong from Paarl, South Africa, in February 2026, estimating its brightness at between magnitude +2.5 and +3.5 at its brightest, according to Spaceweather.com.

Maley reported that the spacecraft was easily visible to the naked eye under dark, moonless skies, but noted that it could also become much fainter, potentially dropping to magnitude +6.

To give yourself the best chance of spotting Shenlong for yourself, head somewhere dark, away from city lights.

Shenlong is a reusable spacecraft that launches aboard a rocket before eventually returning to Earth for a runway landing, much like the U.S. military's X-37B space plane.

China has revealed relatively little about its activities, although the spacecraft has been observed interacting with other objects in orbit. Just days ago, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency released a remarkable new photograph of Shenlong, offering a rare glimpse into this mysterious spacecraft.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

The vehicle, named Apeiron, was flown from Virgin's Arizona manufacturing site to Spaceport America in New Mexico.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Virgin Galactic's first "Delta-class" space plane just made its maiden voyage.

The next-gen suborbital vehicle, named Apeiron (Greek for "Boundless"), lifted off for the first time ever on Thursday (Oct. 28). Flying beneath the wings of its carrier aircraft, VMS Eve, Apeiron traveled from Virgin's manufacturing site in Mesa, Arizona, to its launch site, Spaceport America in New Mexico.

"Seeing the ship fly beneath Eve to Spaceport America was a moment years in the making," Virgin Galactic CEO Michael Colglazier said in a statement on Thursday. "To our team and our astronaut community: your Spaceship has arrived."

Apeiron will undergo a series of checks and tests at Spaceport America, leading up to a planned start of commercial service in the spring of 2027.

During those customer flights, Eve will carry Apeiron to an altitude of about 45,000 feet (13,700 meters), then drop the space plane. Apeiron will fire up its onboard rocket motor, which will carry the six-passenger, two-pilot vehicle to suborbital space.

Passengers will experience a few minutes of weightlessness and get to see the curve of Earth against the blackness of space before coming down for a runway landing back at Spaceport America.

Virgin Galactic has done this before, with its VSS Unity space plane. Unity flew seven commercial suborbital missions during its operational life, which ran from June 2023 to June 2024.

Apeiron and other Delta-class planes are built for a much heavier workload, according to Virgin Galactic.

"Designed to fly twice per week with a vehicle lifetime of more than 500 missions, each Spaceship in the next-generation fleet is built to support the economics of a scaled commercial operation, with increased flight cadence and a cost profile unprecedented in the industry," company representatives wrote in the same statement.

And there will indeed be a fleet, if all goes to plan. The second Delta ship is under construction, for example, and is expected to enter service in mid-2027, according to Virgin Galactic.

Apeiron and its Delta-class siblings will need to fly a lot to deal with Virgin Galactic's backlog: Nearly 700 ticket-holders are currently waiting to fly, according to the company. And demand remains high; the latest batch of seats, which were priced at $750,000 apiece, sold out. Virgin plans to sell the next tranche of tickets for $850,000 each, LATTE Luxury News reported.

When Apeiron gets up and running, it will be the only game in town for suborbital space tourists.

Virgin Galactic once shared the skies with Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin, which flew paying customers to the final frontier on its New Shepard vehicle. New Shepard conducted 14 crewed suborbital flights between July 2021 and January 2026 but is currently grounded while the company focuses on helping NASA land Artemis astronauts on the moon.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. #665. Smithsonian scientists just recreated the first 2 billion years of the Universe

Scientists have created one of the largest and most detailed simulations of the early universe ever developed, offering a remarkable new way to explore how the cosmos evolved after the Big Bang. Known as "Lumina," the simulation was built by researchers at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian to help astronomers interpret observations from powerful instruments such as the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Nancy Roman Space Telescope.

The research, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, reconstructs the universe's first 2 billion years by modeling the interactions between ordinary matter, dark matter, and radiation. By comparing Lumina's predictions with observations from JWST, Roman, and other telescopes, scientists can evaluate how well existing theories explain cosmic evolution and identify discoveries that might challenge their understanding of the universe's fundamental laws.

Astronomers have spent centuries studying the sky and developing explanations for the formation of stars, galaxies, and other cosmic structures. Modern supercomputers now make it possible to turn these ideas into detailed simulations that predict how the universe should behave. When telescope observations agree with those predictions, they strengthen confidence in current theories. Unexpected differences, however, may point toward physical processes that scientists have yet to fully understand.

"With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics," said lead author Oliver Zier, an ITC Fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. "To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video."

Recreating the Universe's First 2 Billion Years

Lumina is the largest cosmological radiation hydrodynamics simulation ever produced. In simple terms, it uses powerful computers to calculate how gas, dark matter, and light influenced one another as the young universe developed. By following these interactions across the first 2 billion years after the Big Bang, researchers can examine how the earliest galaxies formed and how their activity changed the enormous clouds of gas surrounding them.

The simulation models a volume of space more than 100 times larger than those covered by earlier comparable projects. Its virtual universe spans a cube approximately 1.5 billion light-years on each side, providing a view of cosmic evolution on a scale comparable to the vast regions that today's most advanced telescopes can study.

Another major advance is Lumina's treatment of helium reionization, a process in which radiation strips electrons from helium atoms. For the first time, a simulation of this kind follows that transformation as it unfolds while simultaneously accounting for how it affects the surrounding universe. This allows scientists to study the relationship between evolving galaxies, radiation, and the gas that fills the space between them.

"We feel incredibly fortunate to be building simulations like Lumina," said Aaron Smith, an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas and an author on the paper. "For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation."

A Massive Supercomputer Powers the Virtual Cosmos

Recreating such an enormous portion of cosmic history demanded extraordinary computing resources. The team used more than 15,000 graphics processing units on Frontier, one of the world's fastest supercomputers, housed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

That processing power enabled the researchers to simulate an exceptionally large region of the early universe without sacrificing the fine detail needed to investigate individual galaxies and other important structures. As a result, Lumina can capture the broader evolution of the cosmos while also tracking processes involved in the formation of stars, galaxies, and black holes.

Testing the Mysteries of the Early Universe

Beyond recreating cosmic history, Lumina provides a powerful new framework for investigating how the universe developed. Researchers plan to use it to explore the movement of gas between galaxies, the influence of radiation left over from the Big Bang, and the emergence of regions where stars formed at especially high rates.

By placing these predictions alongside observations from the James Webb Space Telescope, the Nancy Roman Space Telescope, and other instruments, scientists hope to build a more complete picture of the universe's earliest chapters. Any unexpected differences between the simulated cosmos and the real one could provide valuable clues, potentially revealing where current theories need to be refined or reconsidered.

#664. What tech entrepreneurs can teach scientists about failure

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dom Byrne is a freelance radio and podcast producer based in Brighton, UK.

Mary Ryan discusses what industry can teach academia about failure in science. Your browser does not support the audio element.Download MP3See transcript

Are universities doing enough to help students learn from their mistakes, and allowing them to see setbacks as a spur to creativity and success?

Materials scientist Mary Ryan, Vice-Provost (Research and Enterprise) at Imperial College London, argues that a good training in science should accommodate learning from setbacks, wrong moves and false starts.

Too often, students judge themselves harshly by one poor exam result or failed experiment, she suggests.

In April 2026 Ryan addressed Failure in Science, a conference held at Imperial in partnership with Nature. In the third episode of a six-part podcast series that revisits some of the conference themes, she says: “People often point to California’s Bay Area as being this hotbed of innovation.

“You can very easily be a serial startup creator there. When you talk to entrepreneurs, one of the first things they tell you is the three companies that they had that failed. That doesn’t preclude them starting a new one and getting funding for it, whereas I think in the UK and probably in Europe in general, there’s more of a requirement for a track record.

“We have to shift that dynamic if the rest of the world is going to catch up with what’s happening in the US.”

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03485-2

I’m Dr. Stephen Webster, director of the Good Science Project at Imperial, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don’t.

And in episode three of Failure in Science, a podcast series about how to do science better, we explore failure and institutions.

Yes, we all have our personal failures, our bad times.

But what if it is actually our institutions that are failing us?

What if a rigid system of education is stifling our imagination?

What if the hunt for grants makes us play safe and narrows our thinking?

Jem Woods, who’s a professor at Imperial College London, opened the Failure in Science conference in April with a quote from Albert Einstein:

The quote is, “As our circle of knowledge expands, so does the circumference of darkness surrounding it. And we have to continue to keep on thinking around and being critically reflective on that uncertainty and the parameters of that uncertainty and how we perceive what we know and what we don’t know.”

And I think that sits at the heart of the failure in science questions.

Yes, I’m Mary Ryan. I’m the Vice Provost for Research and Enterprise at Imperial College London, and I’m the Armourers and Brasiers’ Chair for material science.

So what would I say my big failures are? When you see someone who’s clearly, you know, a successful academic?

You know, I have a research group at Imperial College, so in some ways, I’ve been very successful.

And I think it’s hard, particularly for early career researchers, to see people who have you know, quotes, “made it,” reflecting that they had failures.

So I think actually it’s really important that we talk about things that we weren’t successful at.

Every academic has got a folder on their computer of proposals that were rejected, papers that were rejected for one reason or other.

That doesn’t mean those ideas weren’t worthy or valuable.

Some of them were bad, and we had to be told they were bad.

But how you respond to that rejection? I think failure and rejection are intimately entwined, right?

And that shapes who you are as a scientist, actually, how, that you get them, but how you respond to them.

But there are many times where you do an experiment with a certain focus, and that experiment itself might fail, or you miss something in the background.

Famously, in the 1980s and early 90s, everybody that was working on surface science STM. Many surface science approaches would use highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG) as a standard substrate.

To make your surface clean, what we did, we’d use a piece of tape. We cleave the surface because graphite cleaves very nicely, as we know.

For about 10 years, literally thousands of people were throwing away bits of graphene on their Sellotape because we were focused on the surface and not what we’d done to clean the surface.

And of course the discovery of graphene using exactly that technique was awarded the Nobel Prize.

And I think that’s just a really interesting reflection that you can be doing a certain piece of work and that is successful, but sometimes you’ve also thrown away what was important.

I think that’s a metaphor for life, probably. By focusing on one thing, you throw away what’s really important.

So at the conference, Professor Jem Woods quoted Einstein’s discussion around the kind of, the circumference of knowledge and what is known and what is not known.

And it’s really challenging from an educational training perspective to get that balance of supporting students to understand what we know, but also understanding that there’s uncertainty at the boundaries of that knowledge.

It’s challenging because that makes assessment more difficult. And there’s a large degree of assessment built into how we teach and train and educate people.

But it’s difficult because it becomes very uncomfortable for both the educator and the student to deal with a space where we just don’t know.

Now, I actually think it’s a brilliant opportunity for thinking about how we design education to really put some of those challenging questions into the hands and minds of students, because I think it’s when there are “What are the big questions of the universe?”

You know, they’ve inspired people for generations. And we’ve still got them.

There’s a danger that we now treat education and knowledge as complete when it’s not. And that means that you’re probably not lighting some of those sparks that we’ve seen before.

I think it’s also really, really important that in a space where knowledge is also increasingly captured and categorized by AI, that there’s a real understanding of people that we train that we don’t have the sum total of knowledge.

We don’t know everything. There’s still uncertainties. There’s still questions.

So you’ve also got to question (when you interact with frontier technology) about what if the knowledge you are being told, what knowledge it has been trained on, what is the boundary of that knowledge as well?

So all of those things mean we have to, I think, bring it further into the centre, what is unknown, before we build on what we do know.

So science is founded on experimentation and with the risk of failure fundamentally at its core.

I’m really, curious, I guess, about the balance between applied science and curiosity-driven, sometimes called fundamental science.

And yet, I wonder, aren’t we all curious? And isn’t it that we all want to be curious?

Isn’t that what drives experimentation and testing and knowledge and knowledge generation?

We’re constantly thinking about narrowing our boundaries.

How do we set our boundaries? And yet, we should always be thinking about how we expand our boundaries, how we remain curious.

Professor Jem Woods made an interesting point at the conference around expanding knowledge and this kind, a bit of a tension between discovery, applied science, and how we think about experimentation in that space.

One of the things I like to just try to take everything back to is when you’re thinking about science and applied science, what are the questions you are asking?

Are you asking a why question? Are you asking a what question? Are you asking a how question?

Because that sort of shapes what kind of an experiment you would design and think about.

If you were to take a, you know, a big step back and think about you know pushing the boundary of discovery science, which are often why questions.

And you have a hypothesis or an idea about you know what the answer is to the why, you should always design your experiment to disprove that hypothesis, right?

That’s the way that science actually progresses.

So you should be designing experiments in some ways that fail, right?

Because you’re testing to get to disprove a hypothesis.

I feel like we’ve lost a little bit of that because those experiments are hard to do. They’re hard to think about. They’re hard to publish.

And so what are the mechanisms, by the way, we capture those disproving of hypotheses as really parts of contribution to knowledge.

Because they narrow down what are the right answers and what are the right ways forward.

I still think we need to make sure we capture that as a really fundamental part of the scientific method when we’re doing our training of students.

But quite often, if you want to really, but again, push the boundaries of what you’re going to be able to deliver, you have to work out where those boundaries are, right?

So you have to get to the point where something doesn’t work to understand what does work.

And I think all of those are places where you start to see, and I’m slightly using works and doesn’t work as a failure version, which is not quite the same.

But I think it’s important that you get to the point when you’ve pushed it as far as you can, the frontier of discovery or applied science.

I’m Roseanne. So I’ve been at Imperial for around four years now.

So I think the failure in education session was very relevant to me because I’ve lived it.

So what I really thought was quite inquisitive was this tension between systemic and individual failure, and how the system might, kind of, create individual failure, but then individual failure can kind of symbolize this systemic failure too.

But I felt that what was really important was to make known to students that failure always carries loads of weight and symbolism within our day-to-day lives, but it doesn’t necessarily mean that we’ve failed.

So during the final plenary session, Rosanne I think, fed back on the failure in education.

And she talked really interestingly about the difference between systemic and individual failures.

And I feel like the failure in education discussion really symbolized this first step towards acknowledging, number one, that education is kind of underpinned by inequalities.

That means that other people might not have the right science capital or kind of social capital to mean that we all carry the same equal understanding of science, and that means that we need to bridge these gaps.

But also at the same time that we need to fulfill students with confidence to be able to, not fail, but to make mistakes that result in improving and acknowledging that failure isn’t failure as we like to symbolize it, but how it drives you towards creating....

One thing that really resonated with me and what she was talking about was this idea that at an individual level, the impact of failure is not equally felt.

And the likelihood of failure is not equal, depending on your social capital, your background, the disparity that we have in educational inputs, and the disparity that failure or perceived failure has on your educational outputs, and your life chances.

And this is a really big challenge for all of us, I think, to deal with as a society and as an education community, how do we level that playing field on the way in, and make sure that we are enabling the brightest people, wherever they come from, with a background, to be able to have an equal chance of success?

But then also on the other side of that, some people are allowed to fail, and still succeed, right? And we know we all recognize that in life. We all have experiences of that.

One of the things I think this is it really incumbent on educational establishments is to think about building resilience.

Right, building resilience in our students so they don’t feel that a single failure of a single exam is a reflection on the totality of what they bring, on their talent and their knowledge and what they’ve been learning.

That actually, it’s seen as a space for increased learning, a space to reflect and go back and say, “Actually I can do better.”

Of course, we live and our systems, I think it’s where it comes to the systemic part. Our systems are built on a, you know, pass fail first two one.

And I think what we need to reflect a little bit on is how we talk about that.

I mean, I think you know I am I am still a believer that we need to train people to the highest level they can, and we need to say that we are bringing the brightest and the best, and giving them as the best education they can, in order that they can go on and change the world, right?

But how do we say within this pool of people, everybody is valuable, and everybody’s contribution is valuable, and your output is going to go on and make a difference.

I guess thinking about why it’s important that we actually embrace the idea of failure has got many, many different reasons in it within a university and education context.

One is, I think, the perception of what success looks like for an early career researcher.

There is still a lingering, if you start off doing research, the ultimate endpoint view is to be an academic professor.

We know the likelihood of that is probably about 5%.

But also we know they’re not necessarily the most impactful jobs, right?

And so one thing that we’ve been doing at Imperial is establishing a new research institute for early career researchers that helps them see multiple pathways.

So what does it look like to have a job in industry? What does it look like to work in policy? To work in publishing? To work in the public sector?

And then think about what are the steps that might get you to those kind of careers very early on, not as a second choice, but as actually “That’s my north star from day one. This is what I want to do with my research.”

And that’s an important reset on expectations and the expectations that you give yourself and the expectations that we, as an organization, give to early career researchers that are here.

The other area I think is really important is on innovation and entrepreneurship.

Those are inherently areas that are high risk.

They should be high risk, and they should be, you know, we talk about failing fast.

What we also find is that when you’re in an academic culture, students don’t like to fail.

You know, you don’t want to fail an exam, you don’t want to fail a test.

So, what we’ve done with our entrepreneurship for our undergraduate programme, we’ve set that up through an entity we call the Enterprise Lab.

We have programmes that train students to think about entrepreneurship, how to bring an idea and turn it into a device or a company.

We link them to entrepreneurs outside of the university.

All of that is deliberately extracurricular, right? So it’s not counted for credit.

They can come in, they can explore their ideas. They can be stupid ideas. They can be brilliant ideas.

But they’re not in a framework where someone’s going to give them an A or a B or a C. They’re going to say, “Did I make a company? Did I not make a company? Did I decide I want to do that? I didn’t want to do that.”

And so it completely changes the culture of how they. Approach that activity, and that’s really important for it to be almost like a safe space to fail.

Or almost a place where failing is one of the positive outcomes because you’ve done something that was disruptive and it didn’t work, and that’s a good outcome.

And now you take that and you take it back to somewhere else.

So creating that culture of, you know, have an idea, try something, fail fast. No consequences other than you learnt something, right?

It’s a really important part of how we think about entrepreneurship.

What are the systems questions around innovation spinouts and failure?

People often point to the to the Bay Area, the US, as being this hotbed of innovation, and one of the reasons for that is you can very easily be a serial startup creator, and you have a startup then it fails, and a startup then it fails.

And in fact, when you talk to entrepreneurs in the Bay Area, one of the first things they tell you is the three companies that they had that failed.

That doesn’t preclude them starting a new one and getting funding for it, whereas I think in the UK and probably in Europe in general, there’s more of a requirement for a track record.

So people who have had multiple startups, typically they’ve all succeeded, right?

And so it’s this difference between at a systems level, how you perceive that failure as being “Well, this is my only one chance, so I’ve got to make it work,“ versus, “I’m going to try three or four times until that one works."

We have to shift that dynamic if the rest of the world is going to catch up with what’s happening in the US.

That means a few things. It means probably more venture capital, venture capital is able to take more risk, but also again that resilience in our individuals.

That if this one thing doesn’t work, they should try again and try again.

Can you see the "cat's head" in this nebula?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This "cat's head" would work perfectly in a witch's cauldron, glowing red "eyes" and all.

Just in time for Halloween, we have new, ghostly views of the Cat's Eye Nebula haunting the outer reaches of the cosmos.

This nebula earned its name from its distinctive "cat's head" shape, which you can see on the left-hand side of these two images snapped by both the Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes. In these new images, you can even see the cat's glowing red "eye," which experts suggest could be a young star trapped in the nebula's dusty clutches.

Found about 7,500 light-years away from Earth, this star-forming region can be found within the larger Carina Nebula.

As the stars in the Carina Nebula continue to form, grow and evolve over time, the Nebula itself will change and eventually, this "cat's head" won't look much like a cat anymore. But for now, we can enjoy this vision of a domestic cat somehow depicted in this colossal tour of gas and dust.

As a special Halloween treat, we have not one, but three new images of the cosmic cat's head.

In the snapshot captured by Hubble, we can see the nebula in visible light. This view shows the nebula as a brown pillar of dust embedded in a hazy, almost rainbow field of dust and gas. These colors are captured through Hubble's filters that can see the light coming from oxygen, hydrogen and sulfur and the light scattered by nebula dust.

JWST also took a look at this cat's head, observing the nebula in near- and mid-infrared wavelengths.

By looking at the same objects in space through different wavelengths and with different instruments and telescopes, we can uncover completely new and different details about these far-off celestial objects.
