Richard Schiffman is an environmental journalist in New York City.

A huge lithium-mining operation in Chile’s Atacama Desert.Credit: AP Photo/Rodrigo Abd/Alamy

The Elements of Life: How Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Potassium Nourish Us and Threaten the Planet Kerstin Hoppenhaus Greystone (2026)

The Vanishing Earth: Dispatches from the Frontiers of Extraction James Crawford Bloomsbury (2026)

For much of human history, our species has treated Earth as an inexhaustible source of raw materials. In the past half-century, people have taken more resources from the natural world than in our entire previous history. And the rate of extraction is rising as the global population grows.

Oil and gas drilling is shifting to the deep sea — here’s what is at stake

Oil and gas drilling is shifting to the deep sea — here’s what is at stake

Two books argue that we need to put the brakes on our unsustainable use of resources. In The Vanishing Earth, historian and journalist James Crawford recounts his travels to five landscapes that have been reshaped by drilling and mining.

And, in The Elements of Life, science journalist Kerstin Hoppenhaus examines the three elements vital for plant growth: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Both books are informative and non-technical primers on humanity’s ever-increasing use of Earth’s dwindling resources.

Crawford developed an early interest in the impacts of mining as the son of a mechanical engineer who worked in extractive industries around the world, from the coal beds of Scotland to copper mines in Zambia and oil rigs in the North Sea. He is far from being the first to raise such concerns. First-century Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder wrote of how mining operations “urge us to our ruin” and wondered “when will be the end of thus exhausting the earth”.

Today’s industrial mining operations are on a scale Pliny could have hardly imagined, creating vast toxic areas called sacrifice zones that are, in some cases, uninhabitable. Crawford observed this at first hand when he visited the salt flats of the Atacama Desert in Chile, one of the world’s largest reserves of lithium. Lithium batteries are used in technologies from smartphones to electric vehicles, and demand for the element is expected to rise 50-fold by 2040, which would far outstrip our current ability to extract it.

How fertilizer shortages caused by the energy crisis threaten food security

How fertilizer shortages caused by the energy crisis threaten food security

In Chile, Crawford reports signs that the brine that is the source of lithium salts is already running out, threatening the wider ecosystem with collapse. Indigenous communities in the area are also finding that their water sources are drying up as mining activities deplete reserves stored in the underlying aquifer. The vast Salar de Atacama wetland, which is inhabited by three species of flamingo, might soon become a dead zone, unable to support aquatic life.

Some of the most common resources are also the most overexploited, the author contends. Global demand for clean water has doubled since 1960 and it is predicted that, by the middle of this century, nearly two-thirds of the world’s population will experience water stress, as intensive agriculture depletes aquifers and droughts become more frequent because of climate change. In cities, especially in arid areas, these problems can be exacerbated. Nearly all of China’s major cities are sinking because of subsidence resulting from aquifer depletion, and water shortages have imperilled cities from São Paulo in Brazil to Cape Town in South Africa. Such pressures have inspired schemes to tow icebergs from polar regions, but none has yet been implemented. Failure to tackle these issues could have catastrophic consequences. Struggles over water are projected to become a source of global conflict: water was once dubbed “the petroleum of the next century” in a report by the investment firm Goldman Sachs.

After water, sand is the world’s second most widely used resource. Crawford finds that it is also being over-extracted, as beaches worldwide are mined to meet the demand for construction concrete, which uses sand as its main ingredient. In Vietnam’s Mekong River Delta, intensive sand removal has caused whole sections of coastal farmland to collapse into the river and the ocean. Sand extraction in Sri Lanka has destroyed beaches, exacerbating the impact of sea-level rise and increasing the destructive power of the deadly 2004 tsunami. In India, illegal sand-mining operations have become so lucrative that they are a mainstay of organized crime.

The end of phosphate mining in Nauru has left behind a barren landscape of pinnacles.Credit: Auscape/UIG/Getty

Oil and other fossil fuels are unlikely to run out any time soon, but continued drilling poses a threat to biodiversity and human health. In the Ecuadorian jungle, for example, Crawford describes how chemicals released by drilling have caused cancer rates in the worst polluted areas to rise precipitously. In 2023, Ecuador became the first country where a citizen referendum voted to keep the oil in the ground, after previously becoming the first nation to grant legal rights to the natural world. Nevertheless, drilling continues for now in Ecuador, which, Crawford writes, has “tied its entire fate to oil”.

What can be done? Some environmental damage is inevitable when natural resources are extracted, but Crawford calls for a “repair revolution” to restore blighted landscapes. There is no such thing as “sustainable extraction”, he writes, but there must be “life … after extraction”.

#646. NASA’s Artemis I mission reveals surprising radiation levels near the Moon

NASA's Artemis I mission has provided new insights into how much cosmic radiation astronauts may encounter near the Moon compared with low Earth orbit. Using experimental detectors made from lithium fluoride crystals aboard the Orion spacecraft, researchers have obtained preliminary measurements that reveal unexpected differences in radiation exposure between the two environments.

During the uncrewed Artemis I mission in late November and early December 2022, Orion traveled around the Moon carrying more than 10,000 tiny crystals embedded inside two human-shaped mannequins. These devices recorded radiation exposure throughout the journey. Among them were several dozen experimental fluorescent lithium fluoride detectors created by scientists at the Institute of Nuclear Physics of the Polish Academy of Sciences (IFJ PAN) in Cracow. The researchers have now described a new method for analyzing the information stored in these crystals, offering insights into both cosmic radiation levels and the performance of the detectors. Their findings were published in the journal Radiation Measurements.

"The fluorescent radiation dose detectors based on lithium fluoride, developed at our institute, are passive in nature. In other words, they work like photographic film: once the crystals have been exposed to radiation, the tracks left by individual particles must be analyzed optically under a microscope," explains Prof. Pawel Bilski (IFJ PAN), one of the co-authors of the paper.

How Tiny Crystals Detect Cosmic Radiation

The lithium fluoride detectors work by capturing microscopic changes caused by radiation. When electrically charged particles pass through a crystal, they disrupt its internal atomic structure, creating defects known as color centers. Scientists can later illuminate the crystal with blue light, causing these altered regions to glow red. By examining that fluorescence under a microscope, researchers can identify the paths taken by individual radiation particles.

The detectors were part of the MARE (Matroshka AstroRad Radiation Experiment) study conducted during Artemis I. Several dozen experimental lithium fluoride detectors were placed inside both mannequins, including some containing high concentrations of the lithium-7 isotope. The contribution from IFJ PAN extended beyond these experimental devices. Its scientists also supplied nearly 600 thermoluminescent crystal detectors, which use a different technique to measure radiation exposure.

One major advantage of the new lithium fluoride detectors is that they simplify the process of examining radiation tracks. Traditional passive detectors made from plastic require chemical etching before scientists can study the marks left by incoming particles. Lithium fluoride crystals eliminate that step, allowing researchers to inspect the tracks directly with a standard fluorescence microscope.

As a result, observing the radiation tracks collected near the Moon was relatively straightforward. The more difficult task was determining exactly what those tracks revealed about radiation exposure. To obtain reliable numerical measurements, the team had to develop sophisticated calibration and analysis techniques.

Why Measuring Deep Space Radiation Is So Difficult

Unlike the controlled conditions of a laboratory, cosmic radiation is highly unpredictable. In a typical physics experiment, researchers can expose a detector to a beam containing a known type of particle with a specific energy and direction. In space, radiation arrives from every direction and includes many different particles and atomic nuclei traveling across an enormous range of energies.

This complexity makes the microscopic tracks difficult to interpret. Because incoming particles strike the crystals at different angles, their tracks extend in multiple directions. A microscope captures the section of each track within its focal plane (approximately one micrometer in size), but it also records a blurry glow from portions outside that narrow region. This additional light influences the measured fluorescence intensity, which scientists use to estimate how densely a particle ionizes the material.

Different particles also produce very different track patterns. Those that cause strong ionization leave continuous, sharply defined lines, while particles that produce weaker ionization may appear as scattered, disconnected dots. These differences further complicate the task of translating fluorescence measurements into meaningful radiation data.

To overcome these challenges, the researchers introduced several corrections and developed software capable of removing unwanted background signals. The improved analysis brought their measurements into close agreement with results from established detector technologies while also revealing radiation events that older devices could not detect.

"After applying a series of corrections and developing software to appropriately remove the background interfering with the measurements, our results differed by no more than 15% from those obtained using conventional track detectors across the entire overlapping range of energy deposition values. Moreover, we also recorded numerous particle tracks corresponding to energy deposits below the detection threshold of the detectors used to date," Prof. Bilski emphasizes.

Artemis I Reveals a Surprising Difference in Moon Radiation

The Artemis I measurements also allowed researchers to compare radiation exposure near the Moon with findings from an earlier experiment aboard the International Space Station.

More than a decade before Artemis I, the MATROSHKA experiment investigated radiation exposure using human-shaped mannequins on the space station. Some of the radiation recorded during that mission came from low-energy protons trapped within Earth's Van Allen radiation belts. As these particles traveled into the mannequins, they deposited energy at different depths, producing an uneven distribution of radiation doses.

Conditions near the Moon are substantially different. The Van Allen belts do not extend into the lunar environment, so the radiation encountered there contains a greater contribution from high-energy particles originating elsewhere in the galaxy.

These galactic particles carry enough energy to travel through the entire human body, releasing only a portion of their energy as they pass. Consequently, the Artemis I detectors recorded radiation doses that were distributed almost uniformly throughout the mannequins, unlike the uneven patterns observed in the earlier space station experiment.

The researchers also identified a finding that may seem counterintuitive. Although astronauts near the Moon are exposed to more radiation than those in low Earth orbit, the difference is not necessarily as dramatic as might be assumed.

"Low-energy protons, trapped by our planet's magnetic field within the Van Allen belts, can account for the majority of the radiation dose received by astronauts in low Earth orbit. In the vicinity of the Moon, this substantial contribution disappears. Our measurements from the MARE experiment indicate that, although total radiation doses near the Moon are higher than those in Earth orbit due to the considerable levels of galactic radiation, the difference is not as large as one might intuitively expect," Prof. Bilski notes.

New Radiation Detectors Could Help Protect Future Astronauts

The fluorescent lithium fluoride detectors aboard Artemis I were manufactured using the Czochralski method, a technique for growing crystals. Scientists at IFJ PAN first developed the technology about a decade ago and have continued refining it ever since.

Their compact size is one of their most useful features. Measuring just a few millimeters rather than several centimeters (on the order of millimeters rather than centimeters), the detectors are small enough to be worn comfortably by people, making them practical for monitoring radiation exposure during space missions.

They also provide sharper images of particle tracks than conventional plastic detectors that require chemical etching. This improved resolution allows scientists to distinguish individual tracks even when radiation doses are relatively high. In addition, the crystals can register a broad variety of particle types and energies, potentially providing a more complete picture of the radiation environment.

Another advantage is their ability to detect neutrons, particularly when the crystals are enriched with the lithium-6 isotope. When neutrons interact with lithium nuclei, they can trigger nuclear reactions that generate secondary charged particles. These particles leave detectable changes in the crystal, much like other forms of ionizing radiation.

Together, these capabilities make lithium fluoride detectors a promising tool for studying the complex radiation environment beyond Earth. The measurements from Artemis I offer a clearer picture of how cosmic radiation behaves near the Moon and demonstrate how compact detectors could help scientists evaluate radiation exposure during future missions.

The research conducted as part of the MARE project was supported by a grant from the National Science Centre, Poland (NCN), under its OPUS program.

Living under pressure can significantly impact the cognitive abilities of aquanauts — people living underwater for more than a day.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Our time on our "space mission" underwater was coming to an end, and I felt like what I imagine an astronaut on the International Space Station (ISS) must feel before returning to Earth. On one hand, you are excited to return to your home and loved ones, as well as to fresh food and normal hygiene. On the other, you know you will miss your crew and the incredible experience of being in space.

While my SEA STAR crew and I had not left Earth during our mission, we were separated from the surface of our home planet for five days. All we saw was a green alien water world surrounding us. We did this to live and work like astronauts on the ISS. Instead of dealing with the challenges of space that astronauts face, we problem-solved sometimes equally difficult issues that divers have to manage when performing research in sea water.

Our "wet ISS" was the Jules' Undersea Lab, which is located near Key Largo, Florida, at 22 feet (7 meters) underwater. By the end of our mission, we had all officially become aquanauts. An aquanaut is an undersea explorer who remains underwater for more than 24 hours, without returning to the surface, in a state known as saturation.

In this sense, saturation refers to the physiological condition achieved by a person who breathes underwater long enough for the body's tissues to absorb the maximum possible amount of inert gas (like nitrogen), for a specific depth and pressure. The term aquanaut derives from the Latin word "aqua" (water) and the Greek "nautes" (sailor).

There were a lot of things I wasn't going to miss about being an aquanaut. They included the constant loud noises our life support systems made to keep us alive underwater, as well as bathroom plumbing issues and some health concerns linked to living under pressure. We also had to be very careful when performing our "spacewalks" (scuba dives), due to the low visibility of the environment around us.

Nonetheless, I experienced a sort of "underview effect" during this mission. Most astronauts report experiencing an "overview effect" after seeing our whole planet from space, which usually makes them value our unique planet even more. I felt a similar thing when I saw the sun's rays come through the water. I couldn't reach them, but I enjoyed them from afar. My everyday life felt so close, yet so far away. It gave me both a feeling of longing and more determination to take even more care of our home world than before.

I'm grateful that we were able to perform all of the different scientific projects we planned for our mission. As the Commander of the crew, I usually have my work cut out for me managing the crew and overseeing their research projects, as had been the case for most of the 40 simulated space missions that I led previously. Fortunately, this time my crew was made up of experienced analog astronauts and divers, so the mission was mostly smooth sailing.

The research we chose for this mission was relevant for long-duration space missions. Since we can only send a small number of astronauts to the ISS with a limited number of research activities to perform, underwater stations provide us with a valuable way to conduct analog, or simulated, space missions instead. We also performed some environmental conservation work using a type of underwater vacuum device to help protect the nature around the Jules' Undersea Lab.

My scientific project was focused on studying whether our cognitive abilities and reaction times changed under pressure. This study is part of my collaboration with the Center for Hyperbaric Medicine, Faculty of Medicine of the University of Ostrava and City Hospital Ostrava in the Czech Republic. The whole crew definitely felt like their response times to these tests were slower during the mission than before it.

We were also interested in seeing how microgreens seeds were affected by the changes in pressure. Our Health & Safety Officer, Dr. Brandy Nunez, grew some of our kale and super salad mix before we started our mission, while other seeds started their growth journey underwater. All seeds were transferred to our underwater station using two varied pressure settings (gradual and sudden pressure release during their descent). After we harvested them, we could see that the latter types of seeds did indeed experience some barotrauma (damage caused by the sudden increase in air pressure).

Executive Officer Paul Bakken's work was related to managing the internal pressure of logistical transfer containers when they are exposed to significant environmental changes in pressure. The fourth crewmember, Mission Specialist Jenn Pint, worked with Interstellar Performance Labs to develop a taxonomy for analyzing environmental and crew interaction factors during simulated space missions.

On top of these projects, we also performed neutral buoyancy experiments during our underwater spacewalks, as well as the testing of environmental sensors developed by high school and university students in Slovakia. The sensors provided important supplemental information to the cognitive study about our simulated space habitat's living conditions.

Just like astronauts on the ISS, we dedicated some of our time to outreach and educational work, too. In our case, we called Cosmic Region, a simulated space station in Slovakia, and gave the team there a tour of our underwater habitat. My crewmembers kindly went into the water at that time and performed a spacewalk to show what our work during the mission was like.

As I put on my "spacesuit" (scuba diving gear) one last time, I breathed the stuffy undersea air once more and then dove out to return to "Earth." My crewmembers and I then took a long detour around the lagoon around us to help our bodies adjust to lower pressures. Even though we were only 22 feet underwater, there was still a small risk of decompression-related problems that aquanauts can face after living under saturation for some time. The final step was to breach the surface at long last. That's when we all enjoyed breathing fresh air again and feeling the sun on our faces, though the temperature in Florida made us quickly hide away from it again 😉.

You can follow Dr. Michaela Musilova at her website and on social media: @astro_michaela (Instagram, TikTok and Threads), @Dr. Michaela Musilova (Facebook) and @astro-michaela.bsky.social (Bluesky).

Dr. Michaela Musilova is an award-winning astrobiologist, explorer, professional speaker and author. Michaela has been conducting space-related research at institutions around the world, including NASA, ESA, CalTech, the Canada-France-Hawaii telescope and many others. She was the Commander of 40 simulated missions to the Moon and Mars — the most missions led to date.

#644. Scientists discover a hidden oxygen reservoir deep inside Earth

Scientists have discovered that molten rock deep inside Earth can store far more oxygen than previously believed. The finding challenges long-standing assumptions about magma and raises an intriguing possibility: oxygen released from Earth's interior may have helped transform the planet's atmosphere billions of years ago.

Through high-pressure experiments and advanced computer simulations, researchers found that magma can absorb additional oxygen beyond the amount normally required by its chemical composition. This hidden oxygen could provide a previously unrecognized connection between Earth's deep interior, volcanic activity, and the development of an oxygen-rich atmosphere.

The research was led by Dr. Yanhao Lin and Dr. Ho-kwang Mao of the Center for High Pressure Science and Technology Advanced Research (HPSTAR), working with Prof. Haiyang Niu of Northwestern Polytechnical University and Prof. Wim van Westrenen of Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. Their findings were published in National Science Review.

Scientists Challenge a Long-Standing Assumption About Magma

Oxygen is one of the most abundant elements inside Earth, accounting for more than half of the atoms in the planet's silicate interior. Silicates are minerals and molten materials composed primarily of silicon and oxygen, along with other elements. They make up much of Earth's mantle and crust.

Despite oxygen's abundance, scientists have traditionally assumed that magma can contain only a specific amount of it. Under this understanding, the oxygen content is determined by the quantities and electrical charge states of other elements in the molten rock, including silicon, magnesium, and iron.

Water and carbon dioxide behave differently. Both can dissolve in magma and later escape as gases when the surrounding pressure decreases. These substances are known as volatile components, and their release plays an important role in volcanic activity.

Oxygen, however, has generally not been treated as a separate volatile substance that magma can absorb and release. Whether molten silicate rock could hold additional oxygen independently of its ordinary chemical composition remained largely unexplored.

The new research suggests that this assumption may need to change.

Extreme Pressure Reveals Hidden Oxygen in Molten Rock

To investigate, the scientists recreated conditions found deep within Earth using laboratory equipment capable of generating extraordinary pressures and temperatures.

They heated a synthetic version of mid-ocean ridge basalt, a type of volcanic rock commonly produced where tectonic plates move apart beneath the oceans. The samples were exposed to pressures ranging from normal atmospheric pressure to 7 gigapascals and temperatures between 1200 and 1800 °C.

A pressure of 7 gigapascals is approximately 69,000 times the atmospheric pressure at Earth's surface.

The team used specialized piston-cylinder and cubic presses to maintain these extreme conditions. They also added platinum oxide (PtO2) to establish an oxygen-rich environment and test how much additional oxygen the molten rock could absorb.

After the experiments, the researchers rapidly cooled the molten material, producing glass that preserved important characteristics of the melt. They then analyzed its elemental composition and measured the amounts of water and carbon dioxide present.

By calculating how much oxygen was needed to balance the other elements, along with the oxygen already contained in water and carbon dioxide, the scientists could estimate how much remained unaccounted for.

They called this additional amount "excess oxygen."

The results revealed a striking relationship between pressure and oxygen storage.

At normal atmospheric pressure, the glass contained almost no excess oxygen. At 7 gigapascals, however, excess oxygen accounted for more than 5% of the sample's weight.

For comparison, experiments conducted at similar pressures and temperatures without added platinum oxide produced excess oxygen concentrations of only 0.2% to 0.5% by weight.

The researchers also wanted to determine whether the additional oxygen was truly incorporated into the material or merely trapped as tiny gas bubbles.

Using Raman spectroscopy, a technique that identifies substances by examining how they interact with light, they found no detectable signature of oxygen gas in the glass. This indicated that the excess oxygen had become part of the glass structure rather than accumulating in bubbles.

The measured concentrations may even underestimate magma's actual oxygen-storage capacity. Some oxygen could have escaped while the molten samples were cooling, meaning the original melts may have contained still greater amounts.

Computer Simulations Reveal How Magma Stores Extra Oxygen

To better understand the discovery at the atomic level, Prof. Niu led a series of theoretical computer simulations.

The researchers used deep neural network (DNN) models to simulate interactions among atoms with accuracy approaching that of ab initio calculations, which describe atomic behavior using fundamental principles of quantum mechanics.

The simulations showed that additional oxygen could dissolve into molten material until the system reached equilibrium, a state in which oxygen entering and leaving the melt is balanced.

Although the computer models used a simplified system containing only magnesium, silicon, and oxygen, they reproduced the same overall pattern observed in the laboratory: magma's ability to hold excess oxygen increased with pressure.

The simulated oxygen concentrations were lower than the experimental measurements, which the scientists attributed to differences between the simplified model and the more complex chemical composition of actual basalt.

The calculations also revealed changes in how oxygen atoms behaved as more oxygen entered the melt. Their electrical charges became more varied, and a small proportion formed peroxide-like bonds, in which oxygen atoms bond to one another.

These changes help explain how molten rock might accommodate oxygen beyond the amount predicted by conventional chemical models.

Importantly, the pressure-dependent behavior resembles that of water and carbon dioxide, which also become more soluble in magma as pressure increases.

Based on these findings, the researchers propose that oxygen should be recognized as an independent component of silicate melts, rather than being considered only in relation to other elements.

Could Ancient Volcanoes Have Helped Oxygenate Earth's Atmosphere?

The discovery raises a much larger question about Earth's history: Could magma have transported significant amounts of oxygen from the planet's interior to its surface?

The researchers suggest a possible mechanism involving magma generated in oxidized regions of Earth's mantle.

Under the immense pressures deep underground, this magma could absorb substantial quantities of excess oxygen. As it moves upward, the surrounding pressure decreases, reducing the amount of oxygen the molten rock can retain.

Some of that oxygen could then be released, potentially contributing to chemical reactions that increase the oxidation of the upper mantle, Earth's crust, and eventually the atmosphere.

Oxidation refers to chemical processes involving the transfer of electrons. In this context, oxygen carried by magma could increase the oxidizing capacity of surrounding materials and potentially influence the balance of oxygen in the atmosphere.

This proposed mechanism may also help explain an intriguing coincidence in Earth's geological past.

Between approximately 2.5 billion and 2.0 billion years ago, atmospheric oxygen levels underwent major increases. This interval overlaps with the formation of some of Earth's largest large igneous provinces (LIPs), enormous regions of volcanic rock created by exceptionally large outpourings of magma.

The researchers suggest that oxygen released from these ancient volcanic systems could have contributed to changes in atmospheric composition.

Their preliminary calculation highlights the potentially enormous scale of the process. They estimate that if magma erupted during this period released excess oxygen equal to just 0.27% of its weight, the total amount could theoretically match all the oxygen present in Earth's atmosphere today.

This does not establish that volcanic activity actually supplied that much atmospheric oxygen. Instead, it illustrates how even a relatively small release of oxygen from immense quantities of magma could have major planetary consequences.

A New Clue to Earth's Evolution and Habitable Planets

The findings could influence several important areas of planetary science.

For one, they may change how scientists understand ancient magma oceans, vast regions of molten rock believed to have existed during the early evolution of Earth and other rocky planets.

They also introduce a possible new factor in volcanic degassing, the process through which gases and other volatile substances escape from molten rock and interact with a planet's atmosphere.

If magma can store and release oxygen independently of its other chemical components, models of Earth's atmospheric development may need to account for this previously overlooked process.

The implications could extend beyond Earth. Understanding how oxygen moves between the interiors and atmospheres of rocky planets may help researchers investigate the conditions that allow potentially habitable environments to develop and persist over billions of years.

Although further research is needed to establish how much oxygen natural magmas carry and how much reaches the atmosphere, the discovery points to a surprising possibility: some of the processes that helped shape Earth's oxygen-rich environment may have originated far beneath the planet's surface.

As we all begin to absorb the bitter news of Patrick Stewart's death at the age of 86, a flood of personal tributes are pouring in, reflecting this global treasure's wonderful life lived with a dignity and bravado that few mortals possess.

We’re getting just a hint of what Patrick Stewart meant to those who worked with him or knew him throughout his stellar career. Whether on stage with the Royal Shakespeare Company, on TV as the dashing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," and in Hollywood spectacles like 1984's "Dune," four "Star Trek" feature films, and the many "X-Men" movies in which he portrayed Professor Charles Xavier, Stewart was always the consummate professional. His final screen performance arrives on Dec. 18 with "Avengers: Doomsday" where he’ll present his Charles Xavier character once more.

"Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end," Ian McKellen wrote on Instagram of his "X-Men" co-star and friend. "You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and, in my case, love."

William Shatner, a fellow Enterprise captain, offered his profound sense of loss on Stewart's passing. The legends shared the screen in 1994's "Star Trek: Generations."

"What a heartbreaking week it has been. Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor," Shatner posted on Facebook. "From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work. My heart goes out to Sunny and his family. He will be deeply missed."

Akiva Goldsman, co-creator of Paramount+'s "Star Trek: Picard" and "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds," delivered a sorrowful message in the aftermath of Stewart's death

"Patrick was not only a true lion of the profession, he was the rarest of alchemists, one who could literally turn the written word into flesh and blood," Goldsman wrote. "Patrick was kind, strong, fiercely intelligent, collaborative, vulnerable and wise. His Captain Jean-Luc Picard permanently expanded the universe of 'Star Trek' without measure. He will be deeply missed by this one fan and by so many more."

Stewart's "Star Trek: The Next Generation" family shared their grief and offered up poignant words to try to describe what effect he had on their lives and profession.

"There's no one on this planet that I have acted with or directed more often than my late great friend Patrick Stewart," revealed actor and director Jonathan Frakes, who co-starred for over 35 years with Stewart as Commander Will Riker, in a touching statement. "He will be with me forever. May he rest in Peace."

Finally, Marina Sirtis posted a teary-eyed video in which she explained how much of an impact Stewart had on her life during their time together on "The Next Generation" series and films, in which she portrayed Counselor Deanna Troi beside him.

"Patrick, I loved you with all my heart," she said on Instagram. "I know you're up there now, reunited with all those that you've loved. But to say that you'll be missed down here is probably the understatement of the century. It was an honor to work with Patrick. It was more than an honor; it was the privilege of my life to work with him."

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

#642. Scientists discover a secret glow in toxic fire salamanders

Fire salamanders are among Europe's most recognizable amphibians, known for their striking black and yellow coloring and the poisonous substances they release to deter predators. Despite their familiar appearance, scientists are still uncovering surprising details about their biology. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classifies the species as "vulnerable" on its Red List of Threatened Species. Fire salamanders typically inhabit damp forests, streams, and mountainous regions, where habitat destruction and fragmentation increasingly threaten their survival.

New research has revealed that fire salamanders possess an unexpected ability to fluoresce under ultraviolet light. The glow is most pronounced on the yellow underside of their bodies and along their sides. Researchers traced the fluorescence primarily to glands in the animals' skin and the substances those glands release. Remarkably, these secretions can remain fluorescent for more than 24 hours after leaving the salamander's body.

"It is fascinating that such a well-studied species still harbors unknown phenomena like this. It reminds us that even the most familiar organisms can hide secrets that are only revealed when they are observed with new tools," says Bernat Burriel, a researcher at the Museum of Natural Sciences in Barcelona and the study's first author.

The phenomenon occurs when compounds in the salamander's skin absorb ultraviolet light, which humans cannot see, and reemit that energy as visible light. This process produces vivid green and cyan colors. Known as biofluorescence, it requires an outside source of illumination and should not be confused with bioluminescence. Animals such as fireflies produce their own light through chemical reactions, while fluorescent organisms must first absorb light from their surroundings.

Scientists once believed that biofluorescence occurred almost exclusively in marine organisms, with scorpions standing out as an unusual example on land. More recent studies have challenged that assumption, identifying fluorescent properties in a growing variety of terrestrial animals, including reptiles, birds, and amphibians.

Although researchers have confirmed that fire salamanders fluoresce, the biological purpose of this ability remains uncertain. One possibility is that the glow serves as a form of communication, helping individuals recognize one another or assess potential mates. Another is that it makes their warning coloration more noticeable to predators.

"Fluorescence meets several criteria that suggest a communicative function. It could help salamanders detect each other in nocturnal or particularly dense environments, or act as an additional defense signal," says Martin Kaltenpoth, director of the Department of Insect Symbiosis at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology and a co-author of the study.

The discovery that toxic skin secretions are also fluorescent raises additional questions about how salamanders interact with predators and other animals in their environment.

For now, these proposed functions remain hypotheses. Animals with particularly sensitive vision may be able to detect the green and cyan fluorescence even when it is extremely faint. Humans, however, need a UV lamp to observe the effect.

In the forests where fire salamanders live, nighttime illumination comes primarily from moonlight and starlight. Researchers note that full moonlight contains a greater proportion of ultraviolet and violet wavelengths than daylight, which has a more evenly distributed spectrum. Under these conditions, fluorescence could create small green and cyan highlights against the salamanders' yellow markings, potentially making them easier for other salamanders to spot.

Could the Fluorescent Glow Warn Predators?

Another possible explanation involves aposematism, a defensive strategy in which animals display conspicuous colors to advertise that they are poisonous or otherwise dangerous. Fire salamanders already use their distinctive yellow and black patterns as warning signals, and fluorescence might provide an additional visual cue.

Scientists established a connection between salamander warning colors and chemical defenses more than a century ago when they identified samandarines. These highly toxic steroidal alkaloids are produced from cholesterol precursors and contribute to the animals' chemical protection.

Despite decades of research into salamander toxins and skin chemistry, the newly observed fluorescence came as a surprise.

"The presence of this fluorescent compound was surprising because salamander skin secretions have been studied chemically for decades, and we were unaware of any published reports on fluorescence," says Andrés Brunetti, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology and a co-first author of the study.

One of the biggest unanswered questions concerns the substance responsible for the fluorescence. Researchers have not yet determined its chemical identity, although the evidence suggests it may be a molecule not previously recognized in fire salamanders.

"We still don't know what the compound responsible for this fluorescence is, but everything indicates that it is a molecule unknown until now in this species. Identifying it will be key to understanding its origin and function," adds Salvador Carranza, a researcher at the IBE (CSIC-UPF) and another co-author of the study.

The team is now working to identify and chemically characterize potential compounds responsible for the effect. Determining which molecule produces the glow could help explain how the fluorescence develops and whether it plays a meaningful role in salamander behavior or survival.

A New Discovery With Implications for Amphibian Conservation

Beyond revealing an unexpected feature of a familiar species, the findings demonstrate how new research techniques can uncover biological traits that have escaped scientific attention for decades.

Understanding whether fluorescence influences communication, mating, or predator avoidance could also contribute to conservation efforts. Such information may help researchers better understand the behavior and ecological needs of fire salamanders, which already face significant threats from habitat loss and fragmentation.

The research also involved scientists from the Institute of Subtropical Biology and the Catalan Society of Herpetology. It forms part of a pioneering amphibian conservation project in Catalonia supported by the Barcelona Zoo Foundation.

#641. Meteors don't just burn up. What really happens is far more violent

Scientists have gained a clearer understanding of what happens when rocks from space plunge into Earth's atmosphere and survive the journey to the ground. After examining video recordings and photographs of 75 meteorite falls, researchers identified seven stages that describe how these objects transform into meteorites. Their analysis reveals that melting and breaking apart play a much greater role than previously believed in determining how much material a rock loses, how quickly it slows down, and where its fragments eventually land. The findings were published in the journal Meteoritics & Planetary Science.

"We used to think that solid rocks would evaporate from the enormous heat and brilliant light generated in the air collision," said meteor astronomer and lead author Dr. Peter Jenniskens of the SETI Institute and NASA Ames Research Center. "We found instead that first melting and then fragmentation controls how a rock loses mass."

The researchers determined that incoming space rocks pass through seven distinct phases as they travel through the atmosphere. Different physical processes dominate each phase, influencing the rock's appearance, behavior, and eventual fate.

How Space Rocks Become Bright Meteor Fireballs

The journey begins in Phase 1, high above Earth, where the atmosphere becomes dense enough for the incoming rock to generate a shock wave ahead of it. As the rock collides with air molecules, both its surface and the surrounding gas heat up and begin to glow. This produces the streak of light commonly known as a meteor or "shooting star."

During Phase 2, the meteor travels into increasingly dense air, causing its brightness to intensify. Some meteors also display repeating changes in brightness, which can reveal how quickly they are spinning. Among the fastest rotating objects examined, a complete rotation took between 0.5 and 5 seconds.

One of the documented meteorite falls investigated in this study. Fireball produced by asteroid 2023 CX1 over Normandy, France, on February 13, 2023. Meteorites known as Saint-Pierre-le-Viger reached the ground that day and were subsequently recovered. Credit: Image courtesy of G. de Reijke.

By Phase 3, the meteor has become much brighter, developing into a fireball. At this point, melting becomes the primary process responsible for removing material from the rock. The intense airflow strips molten material from its surface, producing droplets that continue to evaporate after separating from the main body.

"In the laboratory, we cannot generate the amount of radiation that occurs in a natural atmospheric entry at those speeds," said Eric Stern, formerly at NASA Ames and now chief scientist at Hyperspace Technologies, Inc. "Rock could aggressively fragment and erode instead, but then we would not expect the observed systematics in how fireballs brighten."

The fireball enters Phase 4 at an altitude of approximately 60 kilometers (around 40 miles), when melting reaches a relatively stable balance. During this stage, the fireball's brightness either remains nearly constant or increases at a steady rate. According to the researchers, melting alone can ultimately remove as much as 40 percent of the original rock's mass.

Why Meteors Shatter as They Approach Earth

As the fireball descends into denser layers of the atmosphere, increasing air pressure begins to fracture the rock. This marks the beginning of Phase 5, when pieces separate from the main body and can produce repeated bursts of light.

One particularly surprising finding was how early this breakup begins. The researchers found that rocks can start fragmenting when the air pressure acting on their leading surfaces reaches only about one-fifth of the strength measured in meteorites recovered on Earth. They suggest that heating during atmospheric entry, along with cracks left by previous collisions in space, may weaken the rocks enough to explain this unexpected behavior.

It is during this stage that the remaining rock begins shrinking rapidly and experiences substantial deceleration. The more extensively it fragments, the faster it loses speed.

"We were able to tie that slow-down from fragmentation to the previous mathematical descriptions based on ablation," said co-author Stu Pilorz of the SETI Institute.

The researchers also discovered that the shape of the surviving rock can influence where smaller fragments eventually land. If its rear section remains intact, the main body creates an area of reduced pressure in its wake, drawing smaller pieces along behind it.

"Our modeling shows that as long as the back of the space rock remains intact, that rock pulls a vacuum in its wake into which fragments tend to flow," says co-author Darrel Robertson of NASA Ames Research Center. "Those small meteorites fall in a narrow strip on the ground."

The Final Explosion and Journey to the Ground

Phase 6 begins when the rear portion of the main rock finally breaks apart. This last major disruption produces a bright flare and sends fragments scattering at greater relative speeds. Because the meteor has already slowed considerably, these final flashes generally appear red, unlike the bright green colors often observed earlier in its descent.

"That final disruption sends fragments flying at higher relative speeds," said Jenniskens. "In past falls, we noticed that meteorites larger than about 20g tended to be scattered wider and many came from close to the surface of the original space rock, which must have been its backside."

The pieces that ultimately survive to reach Earth's surface began as relatively large fragments. Before landing, however, they experienced additional melting and fragmentation while continuing to lose speed.

During Phase 7, these processes continue until the remaining pieces have slowed enough that they no longer produce visible light. Once melting stops, a thin outer coating known as a fusion crust remains on their surfaces. The darkened fragments then complete their descent, with atmospheric winds potentially pushing them away from their original trajectories before they land as meteorites.

What Meteorite Falls Reveal About Dangerous Asteroids

The researchers examined 75 documented meteorite falls involving several different types of space rock. By comparing their behavior, they were able to determine the altitudes at which different materials entered each of the seven phases.

These observations offer more than an explanation of how small meteorites reach the ground. They also provide valuable clues about the behavior of much larger asteroids, including objects ranging from the size of cars to entire city blocks that can produce powerful explosions in the atmosphere.

By measuring how different solid rocks slow down and fragment during atmospheric entry, scientists can better understand the processes that govern these potentially dangerous asteroid airbursts.

"Asteroids up to tens of meters in size are also solid rocks because they tend to spin faster than do the larger rubble pile asteroids," said Jenniskens. "The 20-m diameter asteroid that caused the airburst over Chelyabinsk, Russia, in 2013 went through the same phases."

SpaceX celebrated Halloween with an early-morning launch from California.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base today (Oct. 31) at 12:04 a.m. EDT (0404 GMT; 9:04 p.m. on Oct. 30 local time), sending 27 of the company's Starlink internet satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO).

The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth as planned, touching down about 8.5 minutes after launch on the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed in the Pacific Ocean.

It was the 18th flight for this particular booster, which is designated B1093. The record for a SpaceX first stage is 37, set this past August by the booster B1067.

The Falcon 9's upper stage did its job as well today, deploying the 27 Starlink satellites into LEO about 62 minutes after launch. They're joining more than 11,000 spacecraft in the Starlink megaconstellation, which is by far the largest satellite network ever assembled.

SDA-T1TL-B | SDA-T1TL-C | Transporter-16 | 14 Starlink missions

Today's launch was the 118th Falcon 9 flight of 2026 so far. More than 70% of these missions have been devoted to building out the Starlink network.

SpaceX has also launched its Falcon Heavy and Starship rockets three times apiece this year. Falcon Heavy is an operational vehicle, but Starship remains in the test-flight phase. The company is currently gearing up for another Starship launch, which is expected to take place sometime in November.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

#639. Scientists just broke a textbook rule of physics

Scientists have pushed X-ray generation beyond a long-accepted limit in laser physics, revealing a surprising quantum effect that conventional theory does not account for. By directing powerful ultraviolet lasers at helium atoms, researchers produced X-rays with substantially higher energies than the standard model predicts. The breakthrough depends on an unusual interaction between two electrons that allows them to release their energy together.

The discovery comes from a collaboration between TU Wien and the University of California San Diego and builds on research that helped establish the field of attosecond physics. Laser techniques developed at TU Wien in the 1990s contributed to advances recognized by the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physics.

For decades, scientists have understood that directing laser light at certain atoms can cause them to emit extremely short pulses of much higher-frequency light, including X-rays. However, the established theory predicts a maximum energy for these emissions based on the properties of the incoming laser. Beyond this boundary, known as the energy cutoff, X-ray production becomes extremely weak.

The new experiment demonstrates that this familiar limit can be exceeded when two electrons interact in a particular way. The findings were published in Nature Photonics.

How Lasers Generate Powerful X-Ray Pulses

"The mechanism behind short X-ray pulses has been well known for a long time," says Prof. Tenio Popmintchev from the Institute of Photonics at TU Wien. "The laser tears a single electron away from the atom. The electron is then accelerated in the laser's electric field until it eventually collides with the atom again. The energy it loses in the process is emitted in the form of light."

During this process, the laser's electric field drives the freed electron away from its parent atom before bringing it back. When the electron returns and releases its energy, it generates light at frequencies far higher than those of the original laser beam.

Nobel laureate Ferenc Krausz used this mechanism in pioneering experiments during the 1990s. Tenio Popmintchev and his colleagues now work at the same TU Wien institute where Krausz conducted his earlier research, but their latest experiment has pushed the process beyond its previously understood boundaries.

"It can be shown that when the electron returns to its atom, it generates a whole range of different frequencies with roughly equal intensity," says Dimitar Popmintchev, postdoc in Tenio Popmintchev's team at TU Wien. "But there is an upper limit. Frequencies above this limit are much weaker; it is simply not possible to exceed a certain maximum frequency."

That prediction describes the conventional process involving a single electron. The researchers wanted to find out whether the outcome would change if two electrons participated instead.

Two Electrons Break the Expected X-Ray Energy Limit

To investigate, the team used intense ultraviolet (UV) laser pulses to interact with helium atoms. Unlike the usual process involving one electron, the experiment allowed both of helium's electrons to be removed in succession.

The first electron was released and accelerated by the laser field, followed by the second. Although the electrons were freed at different moments, their behavior remained connected through quantum correlations. This relationship means their motions cannot be treated as entirely independent.

By carefully controlling the ultraviolet laser pulses, the researchers could arrange for both electrons to return to the atom simultaneously.

"Using UV driving pulses, we can arrange for both electrons to return to the atom at exactly the same time," says Dimitar Popmintchev. "The energy of two electrons is then released all at once. And when more energy is available, a single higher-energy X-ray photon with higher frequency can also be generated."

This coordinated release of energy makes it possible to produce X-ray photons that exceed the conventional energy cutoff. Rather than relying on the energy of a single returning electron, the process draws on the combined energy of two interacting electrons.

An Unexpected X-Ray Signal Confirms the Discovery

The researchers found clear experimental evidence that the two-electron process was producing unusually energetic X-rays.

When they examined the spectrum of the emitted coherent radiation, they identified a second region of sustained emission at much higher photon energies than the standard theory predicts. This additional region, known as a plateau, was weaker than the primary emission but extended well beyond the previously established energy range.

The unexpected signal appeared only when the researchers used helium. Similar experiments involving argon and neon did not produce the same behavior in their outer electrons.

This difference provides important evidence for the proposed explanation. Helium has particularly strong correlations between its two electrons, allowing them to interact in ways that make the simultaneous release of energy possible. The outer electrons of argon and neon did not demonstrate the same effect under the experimental conditions.

Beyond producing higher-energy X-rays, the discovery could give scientists a powerful new way to investigate how electrons interact inside atoms and other materials.

The unusual coherent X-ray emission could serve as a highly sensitive spectroscopic "sensor" for electron-electron correlations. By studying the shape of the emitted spectrum, its maximum energy, and how it changes with the polarization of the laser light, researchers could gain information about the behavior of interacting electrons on extraordinarily short timescales.

These interactions occur over attoseconds, with one attosecond equal to one billionth of a billionth of a second. Observing processes at such speeds is essential for understanding how electrons move and influence one another in quantum systems.

Eventually, the same principle might be extended beyond individual helium atoms to molecules and solid materials in which electrons interact strongly.

The technique behind the discovery, known as high-harmonic generation, originally helped make attosecond physics possible. Now, researchers are finding that it can also reveal the complex behavior of multiple interacting quantum particles.

These insights could contribute to research on quantum computing and help scientists understand and design advanced nanomaterials with carefully controlled properties.

From Saturn's spectacular rings to Halloween fireballs and a space station flyover, there are plenty of celestial treats in store this Halloween. Here's when and where to look.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There could be more than just ghosts and ghouls lurking in the skies this Halloween! From Saturn's spectacular rings to shooting stars and even a space station flyover, the night sky has a few treats of its own in store for U.S. skywatchers on Oct. 31.

Based on the latest national forecast, skies will be mainly clear on Saturday evening over most of New York State, northeast Pennsylvania, northern New Jersey and New England as well as a swath of the southern and central Great Plains, central Rockies, a portion of the Pacific Northwest and central and south Florida, as costumed kids arrive at the door looking for candy or some other Halloween treat.

Temperatures will be mostly in the chilly 40s across the Northeast US, upper 50s and 60s for the nation's midsection, warm 70s to near 80 for the southern US, including Florida and the Gulf Coast, and 40s for much of the western US. Unfortunately, a storm moving across the nation's heartland may spell rainy skies for parts of Iowa and Nebraska, south to the Gulf Coast.

For those blessed with a generally fair evening, there will be views of mid-autumn stars and constellations plus a bright planet shining prominently in the early evening sky. If you plan to accompany children around your neighborhood, you might want to enlighten them by pointing out some of those objects that will be visible in the sky. Better yet, if you have a telescope, give your visitors a treat of a different kind: Give them a close-up view of some of those celestial sights.

At around 7 p.m. local time, tell your young audience to make a clenched fist with their hands and then hold them out at arm's length. Now, tell them to go "two fists" up from the east-southeast horizon and they will see a bright star, shining with a yellow-white hue. Now, direct your telescope toward that "star" and when you gaze through the eyepiece, you will not be looking at a star at all . . . but a planet!

This sixth planet out from the sun, just might be the most beautiful of all. Its rings are still readily evident, although currently they appear somewhat edge-on with the south face tilted only about 6 and a half degrees to our line of sight. A telescope magnifying 30-power will bring them out; they appear to bisect the ball of the planet. While this is far from their appearance compared to other years, the view should still look impressive to those who have never seen the ringed planet for themselves.

Because they are active over Halloween, the Taurid meteor shower is sometimes called the "Halloween Fireballs." The bits of debris that make up the Taurids are a little larger than average, so they can result in brighter meteors and even fireballs, or exploding meteors (called bolides), that streak across the sky and leave incandescent trains in their wake. While they are most active during the second week of November, a few forerunners can show up on Halloween night, darting from out of the east-northeast part of the sky. So, if you or your young visitors see something resembling a flare from a Roman candle sweeping majestically across the evening sky, it may very well be a Taurid meteor.

Not the International Space Station, but the Tianhe-1 core module, the first module to launch of the Tiangong space station. It was launched into orbit on 29 April 2021, as the first launch of the final phase of the Tiangong program, part of the China Manned Space Program (Project 921). On Halloween evening, Tianhe-1 will be following a track from Chicago to New York at an altitude of 240 miles (385 km) and should be readily visible to the naked eye across the Northeast US within a few minutes of 7 p.m. EDT, wherever skies are reasonably clear.

The Tiangong Space Station should appear to resemble a very bright star moving across the sky on a general west-to-east course. For places near and along the flight path, the Space Station will appear to pass almost directly overhead. For those situated south of the track, Tiangong will reach its highest point above the northern horizon; those situated north of the track will see the station peak high in the south.

If you see it, tell your young viewers that three astronauts are currently living and working aboard the Tiangong Space Station, of which the Tianhe core module serves as the main living quarters. If you would like specific details on when and where to see the Space Station from your hometown, check out Heavens-Above, a non-profit website and mobile application that tracks satellites, the International Space Station (ISS), comets, and astronomical events in real time.

Another website that provides live information, including an orbit map on Tianhe-1, is NY2O.com. Check its menu list on the right side of the page and look for the blue box: "10-Day Predictions for CSS (Tianhe-1)."

In the September 2019 issue of The Astronomical League Magazine "Reflector," author Richard W. Schmude Jr., offered some tips for those who plan to do public outreach for astronomy on Halloween:

"Firstly, children sometimes grab or touch the eyepiece, so use an inexpensive one. I gently warn children not to touch the telescope. In my area, parents have learned to tell their children not to touch the telescope. In some cases, a child will grab the eyepiece, causing the telescope to shift. For this reason, a Dobsonian telescope with a good finderscope is a good choice for Halloween outreach. A small stool or booster ladder may help very small viewers. Sometimes, parents hold their children up to look through the eyepiece. One may also place a monitor-connected video camera in the telescope and people can easily see the object on a screen." "Finally," adds Mr. Schmude, "I have my bag of goodies next to my telescope so that the children get two treats!"

Whatever your weather, Happy Halloween from all of us at Space.com!

#637. Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal

Blood pressure readings are typically evaluated based on their average values, but growing evidence suggests that fluctuations throughout the day may be equally important. Rapid or excessive changes in blood pressure can independently increase the risk of heart disease, stroke, and brain injury, even when average readings fall within the normal range.

Researchers at the University of Virginia School of Medicine have identified a small population of nerve cells in the brainstem that helps maintain steady blood pressure. The brainstem regulates essential involuntary functions, and these newly studied cells appear to limit blood pressure swings as people move between everyday activities, including sleeping, waking, standing, and exercising.

"What we found is that a loss of just a few hundred nerve cells leads to unstable blood pressure even though the mean blood pressure was normal," said UVA's Stephen Abbott, PhD, the lead investigator of the study. "This shows that the system that keeps blood pressure steady from moment to moment is no longer working."

A Hidden Brain Mechanism Behind Blood Pressure Problems

The same nerve cells have previously been found to be damaged or missing in people with multiple system atrophy, a rare, fatal neurological disorder related to Parkinson's disease. The condition is often accompanied by severe difficulties regulating blood pressure.

The new findings raise the possibility that disruptions involving these brain cells may also contribute to unstable blood pressure in other medical conditions, including cases where standard measurements show normal average levels. Understanding this mechanism could eventually help researchers develop treatments aimed at reducing harmful fluctuations and protecting against their potential consequences.

"Our work emphasizes a new appreciation for how we think about blood pressure problems," Abbott said. "It's not just about lowering the numbers - it's about keeping blood pressure stable from moment to moment."

New Research Could Change How Blood Pressure Is Treated

The findings were published in the scientific journal Circulation Research. The research team included George M.P.R. Souza, Harsha Thakkalapally, Faye E. Berry, Leah F. Wisniewski, Ulrich M. Atongazi, Daniel S. Stornetta, and Abbott. The researchers reported no financial interests related to the study.

Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health through grant HL148004.

The discovery also reflects the broader goals of UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute focuses on advancing research into difficult and complex diseases while helping promising laboratory findings move more quickly toward potentially lifesaving treatments for patients.

#636. The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought

A major new study has uncovered important differences in how the brains of autistic children respond to human faces. Published in Nature Mental Health, the research is among the most extensive investigations yet into how face perception works in autism.

Some autistic people tend to look at faces less frequently or make less eye contact. They may also find it more difficult to remember faces or interpret facial expressions compared with neurotypical individuals. Scientists have spent decades investigating the brain activity behind these differences. In the early 2000s, for example, researchers at Yale reported that brain regions responsible for processing faces showed lower activity in autistic individuals than in people without autism.

James McPartland, PhD, Harris Professor in the Child Study Center and director of the Center for Brain and Mind Health, studies how autistic people process faces using electroencephalography (EEG), a technique that records the brain's electrical activity. Previous EEG studies, however, have typically examined signals from limited regions rather than analyzing activity across the entire scalp.

To gain a more complete picture, McPartland and his colleagues conducted a study involving approximately 400 autistic children, examining electrical signals recorded across the scalp. They discovered that brain activity associated with face recognition was less clearly distinguishable in autistic participants. They also identified a striking difference in development: In neurotypical children, the brain's response to faces became more specialized with age, while autistic children did not show the same pattern.

"This is the first time we've leveraged the full volume of very rich information provided by an EEG recording to understand face perception and autism," McPartland says.

How Scientists Discovered Differences in Autistic Brain Activity

McPartland compares traditional approaches to studying face recognition with attempting to understand traffic throughout an entire city by monitoring just one downtown street.

"That's the way most research on face processing so far has worked," McPartland says.

The new approach provides a much broader perspective, similar to observing traffic across an entire city using satellite imagery. To investigate these patterns, the researchers analyzed information collected through the Autism Biomarkers Consortium for Clinical Trials (ABC-CT). The dataset included autistic and neurotypical children across different age groups.

During the experiments, participants viewed pictures of faces and everyday objects while EEG equipment recorded their brain activity. Instead of concentrating on a small number of recording locations, the scientists examined electrical signals from all 128 electrodes positioned around each participant's scalp.

They then applied machine learning techniques to determine whether patterns in the recordings could reveal what each child was viewing.

The results showed that brain activity provided a clearer indication of face viewing in neurotypical children than in autistic children. In other words, the electrical signals associated with seeing faces were less distinguishable in the autistic group.

"The neural activity that we measure at the scalp is just not as distinct in autistic children," says first author Jason Griffin, PhD, assistant professor of psychology at University of Houston. Griffin previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in McPartland's laboratory.

The researchers also found that the ability to identify what a child was viewing from brain activity improved with age among neurotypical participants. This age related improvement was not observed in autistic children, suggesting that their neural responses to faces develop along a different pattern.

"Their face-specific processing is not following the same trajectory," Griffin says.

Face Recognition Differences May Begin Earlier Than Previously Thought

Beyond identifying differences in brain activity, the study offers new insight into how early those differences emerge during face perception.

Recognizing someone involves multiple stages of neural processing. The sequence begins when visual information enters the eyes and continues as the brain interprets that information until a face is recognized.

Much of the earlier research on autism and face perception has concentrated on a brain signal called the N170. This measurable change in electrical activity typically occurs about 170 milliseconds after a person sees a face. Previous studies have shown that the N170 response tends to occur later in autistic individuals.

By analyzing brain activity over a wider period, the researchers found evidence that differences in face processing begin before this familiar signal appears. This suggests that autism related differences may arise at earlier stages of visual processing than researchers had previously established.

"But when you look at face processing through an approach that's more inclusive of the full temporal range of information, we're seeing that differences in autism occur even earlier," McPartland says.

What the Discovery Could Mean for Autism Diagnosis and Early Support

The findings could eventually influence how researchers approach autism diagnosis and the development of supportive interventions.

Historically, some clinicians attempted to address difficulties with face perception by requiring autistic individuals to maintain eye contact. Research has since shown that forcing eye contact is not an effective solution. A better understanding of how face processing develops in the brain could help identify approaches that are more useful and appropriate.

An ongoing challenge in autism research is separating neurological differences associated with autism itself from changes that may develop through the experience of living with the condition. According to the researchers, the patterns identified in this study suggest that differences in face processing are connected to underlying developmental characteristics of autism rather than simply reflecting accumulated life experiences.

"When we're seeing this expected refinement and specialization in non-autistic people, we're seeing a reduced developmental change in autistic people," McPartland explains.

Because the differences appear during development, the findings also raise the possibility that support aimed at helping autistic children interpret facial emotions could be particularly beneficial when introduced earlier in childhood.

However, the researchers emphasize that autism does not necessarily create difficulties that require intervention. Many neurodivergent people experience little or no impairment related to their autism and may neither need nor want additional support. For others, challenges with recognizing faces or understanding facial expressions can complicate everyday social interactions.

"Imagine navigating life when it's hard for you to perceive the information in another person's face, from navigating a playground to navigating a job interview," McPartland says. "This is one of the critical areas that causes difficulty for many autistic people."

New Brain Signals Could Help Improve Autism Diagnosis

Another potential application involves the search for more objective ways to assess autism. Currently, clinicians diagnose autism primarily by evaluating behavior because reliable biological tests are not yet available for routine diagnosis.

Scientists are investigating several possible biomarkers, which are measurable biological characteristics that could improve diagnostic assessments or help distinguish different groups within the autism spectrum.

The newly identified patterns of face related brain activity could contribute to that effort. By examining how these neural signals differ among individuals, researchers may eventually develop additional diagnostic tools or better identify autistic people who are likely to benefit from particular forms of support, including social skills therapy.

Although more research is necessary before these findings can be used in clinical practice, the study provides a new way to investigate how the autistic brain processes faces and how those responses change throughout childhood.

"This is a first step in introducing a new biomarker," McPartland says.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Something spooky is stirring in the shadows of the infamous star Betelgeuse, a cosmic poltergeist that is disrupting the atmosphere of the red supergiant.

New radio observations have shown Betelgeuse's smaller stellar companion, Siwarha (not Betelguese Betelguese, unfortunately), cutting through the supergiant's extended atmosphere and leaving a wake in its path, like a jet boat slicing through a lake.

Because the name of this red supergiant star located about 650 light-years away from Earth, marking the shoulder of constellation Orion, is Betelgeuse, which means "the hand of al-Jawza" in Arabic, the companion was named Siwarha, meaning "her bracelet."

"This companion is orbiting so close to the star that it actually passes through its extended atmosphere," Lynn Matthews, the principal research scientist at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Haystack Observatory who led the new observations, said in a statement.

Using data collected from 2021 to 2026 using the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array in New Mexico and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in Chile, Matthews and colleagues found that Betelgeuse's atmosphere stretches into an egg shape when the companion star is farthest away and rounds out when the companion passes in front of or behind it.

The same data also showed that Betelgeuse itself has largely recovered from the "Great Dimming" that made headlines in 2020. This recovery comes after the red supergiant "sneezed" in 2020, dramatically ejecting tons of gas and dust and fading to its dimmest in more than a century.

Among the long-standing mysteries of Betelgeuse, scientists have puzzled over a brightening and dimming cycle that lasts roughly 2,100 days. Recent studies pointed to a low-mass companion orbiting deep inside the star's atmosphere, and its existence was confirmed in early 2026.

Though Siwarha itself is too faint to detect directly at radio wavelengths, its influence shows up in the star's shape, the new study found. To confirm the effect, the researchers say, they will need to observe more of the companion's orbit, especially at radio frequencies that have so far been sparsely sampled.

The Next Generation Very Large Array, a planned telescope, should make this kind of monitoring far more routine, according to the team. With sharper vision, researchers could see how red supergiants like Betelgeuse shed their material as they near the end of their lives, and how a close companion might affect that process by tugging on that ejected matter.

This research is described in a paper published in The Astronomical Journal.

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston.
