#558. Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins

An ancient ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging a long-standing theory about where the ancestors of modern apes, including humans, first evolved. The remarkable find suggests that a crucial chapter of our evolutionary history may have unfolded much farther north than scientists previously believed.

The newly identified species, named Masripithecus moghraensis, lived approximately 17 to 18 million years ago during the Early Miocene. Its fossilized remains were recovered from Wadi Moghra in northern Egypt, making it the first definitive fossil ape ever discovered in North Africa.

The discovery, described in a study published March 26, 2026, in Science, comes from an international team at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center (Egypt) and the University of Southern California (USA). Their findings suggest that northern Africa and the Middle East may have played a central role in the emergence of the evolutionary lineage that eventually gave rise to all living apes.

A Missing Piece of the Ape Evolutionary Puzzle

For decades, scientists believed that early apes and their close relatives were concentrated primarily in regions farther south in Africa. Fossil sites in North Africa had produced remains of ancient monkeys from the Early Miocene, but researchers had never found definitive evidence of apes from the same period.

That gap helped shape prevailing theories about ape evolution. Although younger ape fossils have been discovered across Africa, Europe, and Asia, their evolutionary relationships and geographic origins remain subjects of scientific debate.

The newly discovered Egyptian fossil may help explain what was missing from this picture.

"We spent five years searching for this kind of fossil because, when we look closely at the early ape family tree, it becomes clear that something is missing -- and North Africa holds that missing piece," said Hesham Sallam, a paleontologist at Mansoura University and senior author of the study.

The discovery is especially important for understanding the origins of crown Hominoidea, the evolutionary group that includes the last common ancestor of all living apes and its descendants. Today, that group encompasses gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, and humans.

Scientists suspect that the incomplete geographic distribution of ancient fossils has obscured important details about when and where this group first emerged.

An 18-Million-Year-Old Ape With Unusual Teeth

The fossils were uncovered during expeditions in 2023 and 2024 by researchers from the Sallam Lab at Wadi Moghra, a well-known fossil site in northern Egypt.

The team named the species Masripithecus moghraensis. Its genus name combines Masr (مصر), the Arabic name for Egypt, with píthēkos, the Greek word for ape. The species name honors Wadi Moghra, where the fossils were found.

Although the remains consist only of lower jaw material, they contain an unusual combination of anatomical features that distinguishes the animal from other apes of similar age.

The jaw is exceptionally sturdy, with remarkably large canine and premolar teeth. Its molars also have rounded chewing surfaces covered in pronounced textures. These characteristics offer valuable clues about the foods the animal could eat and how it survived in its environment.

Researchers believe Masripithecus primarily consumed fruit but had teeth powerful enough to process tougher foods when necessary. This dietary flexibility may have been an important survival advantage.

"Together, they suggest that Masripithecus was adapted for versatility. The study interprets its chewing anatomy as evidence of a flexible, mainly fruit-based diet, with the ability to process harder foods such as nuts or seeds when needed. This flexibility would have helped Masripithecus to thrive at a time when climatic changes were leading to more pronounced seasonality in northern Africa and Arabia," said Shorouq Al-Ashqar, a researcher at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center and a first author of the study.

As seasonal differences became more pronounced, the availability of certain foods likely changed throughout the year. An ape capable of eating a wider range of foods would have been better equipped to cope with those fluctuations.

A Discovery That Challenges the Ape Family Tree

The importance of Masripithecus extends well beyond its unusual anatomy. When researchers examined where the species belonged on the evolutionary family tree, they uncovered a surprising result.

Their analysis suggests that Masripithecus was more closely related to living apes than any known ape species from the Early Miocene of East Africa.

To investigate these relationships, the team used advanced statistical techniques known as Bayesian methods. These approaches allow scientists to compare different evolutionary possibilities and estimate how strongly the available evidence supports each one.

The researchers combined anatomical information from living and extinct apes with genetic evidence from living species. They also incorporated the geological ages of fossil specimens, helping them estimate when different evolutionary branches separated.

By bringing these sources of evidence together, the scientists reconstructed relationships among ancient and modern apes and explored where their shared ancestors may have lived.

The results challenge the long-standing assumption that the evolutionary roots of all living apes were centered in or around East Africa.

Could North Africa Be the Birthplace of Modern Apes?

Additional analyses of ancient animal distributions pointed toward northern Africa and the Middle East as the most likely geographic home of the common ancestor of all living apes.

That ancestor is estimated to have lived during the Early Miocene, an interval spanning roughly 23 million to 16 million years ago. This was an important period in primate evolution, when early ape lineages were diversifying, and environments were undergoing substantial changes.

Geography may help explain why this region was so important.

Millions of years ago, Africa, Arabia, and Asia were moving toward a new geological arrangement. As the African and Arabian tectonic plates traveled northward and approached the final stages of their collision with Asia, the connections between these landmasses began to change.

Sea levels also rose and fell, periodically reducing the stretches of water that separated different regions. At certain times, these changes made it easier for animals to move between Africa and Eurasia.

Northern Africa and the Middle East therefore occupied a potentially crucial position in the movement and evolution of ancient mammals, including apes.

The discovery of Masripithecus helps connect previously separated fossil records from Africa and Eurasia. Its presence suggests that apes were already evolving into distinct forms in this region before new land connections made it possible for them to expand into Europe and Asia.

Rather than being a peripheral location in ape evolution, the region may have been an important center of evolutionary diversification.

Scientists Rethink Where Our Ancient Ape Ancestors Lived

The findings have even prompted some of the researchers to reconsider ideas they held throughout their careers.

Erik Seiffert, a paleontologist at the University of Southern California and co-author of the study, explained how the evidence has changed his understanding of ape origins.

"For my entire career, I considered it probable that the common ancestor of all living apes lived in or around East Africa. But this new discovery, and our new and novel analyses of hominoid phylogeny and biogeography, now strongly challenge that idea. And, importantly, the likelihood of this scenario doesn't depend on Masripithecus -- but it is very much consistent with it."

Importantly, the researchers are not claiming that Masripithecus was a direct ancestor of humans or even necessarily the direct ancestor of living apes. Instead, its position on the evolutionary family tree provides evidence about where the broader ancestral lineage may have originated.

The distinction matters because humans emerged much later in evolutionary history. The Egyptian fossil offers clues to an earlier stage, when the distant ancestors shared by humans and other living apes were evolving.

The team's findings also suggest that the traditional emphasis on East African fossils may have provided an incomplete view of this much older evolutionary story.

More Evolutionary Secrets May Be Hidden in Egypt

Although the discovery offers compelling new evidence, scientists still have much to learn about Masripithecus and the early history of modern apes.

Only part of the animal's jaw has been recovered, leaving important questions about its overall appearance, body size, movement, and behavior unanswered. Additional fossils could provide a more complete picture of how this ancient species lived and how it relates to other early apes.

The researchers believe that further exploration of North Africa and the Middle East could reveal additional species and help clarify when and where the major branches of the modern ape family tree began to emerge.

For now, Masripithecus moghraensis offers a striking reminder that even fundamental ideas about our distant evolutionary past can change when scientists uncover evidence in places that have received relatively little attention.

A fossil jaw preserved for nearly 18 million years may be helping scientists piece together a chapter of evolutionary history that was missing all along.

#557. Male Insecurity Over Penis Size Is a Booming Business

Bill Moore is what you might call a televangelist for big dicks.

At AdvancedYou, an anti-aging aesthetic clinic specializing in “biohacking and wellness treatments” that he runs out of a Dallas strip mall, Moore offers men a unique form of personal salvation through PhalloFill. It’s a penis enlargement procedure that, while not able to add inches in length, involves injecting hydrocyanic acid dermal filler for increased girth.

In Daniel Lombroso’s new documentary Manhood, in theaters this week, the director tracks this desperate quest for sexual adequacy among men who find themselves struggling with self-worth and the crisis of modern masculinity.

As headlines about the male loneliness epidemic were making the rounds a few years ago, which Lombroso felt were “sort of thin and maybe navel-gazy,” he decided he wanted to tell a more “propulsive story” about what was going on with men in America. Around that time, he also started hearing more about penile enhancement and began talking to some of the practitioners offering it as well as the men getting it, including Moore, who invited him to Texas.

Moore fancies himself something of a cosmetic revolutionary. He was among the first wellness professionals in Dallas to use platelet-rich-plasma for hair replacement. In Manhood, his goals remain unwavering: to make his patented penis enlargement technique as commonplace as Botox.

You could say Lombroso, a former editorial producer for The Atlantic and The New Yorker, has a metaphorical hard-on for subcultural deep dives. His first documentary, White Noise, followed white-nationalist groups for three years from Donald Trump’s 2016 win until the end of his first term.

With Manhood, Lombroso wanted to understand what was driving men to get on the operating table. During visits to Moore’s clinic, he met men with unique stories: a megachurch pastor; border patrol agents; a man suffering from brain cancer. David, a 24-year-old gay OnlyFans star shunned by his religious mother, who visits AdvancedYou following a botched procedure, and Ruben, an out-of-work father of five who moonlights as a stand-up comedian and listens to the Joe Rogan podcast, are cast as the central figures in the film, along with Moore.

“I was just like, this is fucking crazy that these guys are really eager to tell Bill, and were really eager to tell me, what was going on in their life,” Lombroso says. To his surprise, an overwhelming majority—he estimates around 75 percent—of the men undergoing the procedure were straight. “People for some reason make the assumption that it wouldn't be that division, but it's mostly straight men,” whom he notes were “conservative-leaning.”

Lombroso is careful not to reduce the men seeking penis enlargement to one type but says they all carried a similar trait: “this deep feeling of shame and social isolation.”

Penis size is an unusually intimate subject shaped by cultural ideas about masculinity and self-worth—though not everyone buys into the belief that the size of your penis determines your well-being. In one scene, Ruben talks with a bar patron about the documentary before his stand-up set, explaining that the film is about “mental health” and “normalizing” the procedure, only for the man to respond with gleeful skepticism. “Having a small dick makes you crazy?” he wonders jokingly.

“There’s a limit to what a scalpel and a syringe can provide,” Alex Tatem, a prosthetic urology specialist, says in the film. “I can fill your penis with filler, but I cannot fill the hole in your heart.”

There is a pressure on men to constantly improve, and Manhood suggests that perhaps Moore, despite his seemingly genuine intentions, has exploited that need. His “girth enhancement” procedure, which costs between $2,500 and $4,000 per visit, basically runs like a subscription model where he encourages men to visit three, four, even five times. The catch is that if they want to maintain their desired girth, they have to visit once a year for the rest of their life.

Several subjects in Manhood take injections to increase their girth.

“You would think that this technique would have stayed in the hands of urologists, but now this is something that is in the hands of corporate marauders,” Paul Perito, a board-certified urologist explains in the film. PhalloFill has expanded to 32 clinics across the US.

More men are pushing their bodies to the limit for validation in ways they never did before. They have outpaced women as the fastest-growing demographic for plastic surgery in the US and are undergoing cosmetic procedures at a higher rate compared to years prior to 2020, according to the International Society of Aesthetic Plastic Surgery. Among Gen Z and millennials, nonsurgical cosmetic treatments—everything from skin resurfacing to body sculpting—are growing more widespread.

Nowhere is this trend more pronounced than in the looksmaxxing movement, popular in manosphere and incel circles, where young men are encouraged to undergo extreme physical modifications in order to be more sexually desirable. One 21-year-old looksmaxxing YouTuber I interviewed last year likened the trend to a “looks inflation.”

“It is ridiculous how much it’s meant to be a sign of strength,” one client says, lying on the operating table as Moore pokes tiny needles into the shaft of his penis. “There are even allegations of, like, ‘Oh, a terrorist must have a small dick’ … And you’re a guy, so you’re just gonna take it.”

Morag Yule, president of the Society for Sex Therapy, puts it another way. “Insecurity is big business, and there is money to be made” off people who will “do almost anything to feel better about themselves.”

While Lombroso never paints Moore purely as a villain or savior, it is evident that PhalloFill is part of the larger wellness industry exploiting male insecurities. A 2026 study by researchers from the digital safety organization Reset Tech argued that the manosphere operates more like a pyramid scheme, preying on the vulnerabilities of men like Ruben, who, in the end, ends up pouring so much money into injections that he and his wife are forced to move out of their house and relocate to Phoenix with his “first baby momma.” “We weren’t making enough money to afford everything,” Ruben says.

What ultimately emerges in Manhood is a darker truth about exploitation and profit motives in the medical industry. Doctors and practitioners are recast as cash-thirsty business sharks. “When they see money, that excites them,” Lombroso says. “I think that’s a really unfortunate thing that we don’t talk enough about. A lot of the people in the movie are trained urologists who could be doing penile reconstructions or helping men with [erectile dysfunction]. Instead, they see a quick way to make a buck putting lip filler in people’s dicks.”

#555. Norwegian shares surge 13% on earnings beat, guidance raise

Shares of Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings surged 13% Thursday after the company posted better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and raised its outlook for the full year.

The cruise line reported third-quarter revenue of $2.95 billion, topping Wall Street expectations of $2.88 billion, according to analyst estimates from LSEG.

Net income for the period was $491 million, or $1.07 per share.

Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization was $937 million, which exceeded Norwegian's previous guidance of $874 million. Adjusted EPS was $1.12, exceeding previous guidance of 90 cents and outpacing analysts' expectations of 94 cents, per LSEG.

Norwegian also raised its full-year guidance, citing its stronger-than-expected third-quarter performance. The company now expects 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $2.55 billion and adjusted EPS of about $1.70.

The report said the company's bookings had "improved modestly" since its last report but remain below its optimal range.

Norwegian said it will emphasize new marketing strategies, including the launch of a new marketing platform in January. It also said it anticipates that enhancements such as a new waterpark at its Great Stirrup Cay private island will support stronger demand.

Also on Thursday, Norwegian announced that Chief Financial Officer Mark Kempa will step down after more than 25 years at the company. Meghan Montana, currently chief strategy officer, will take over the role starting Jan. 1.

#554. Elon Musk’s Ties to Texas Republicans Go Much Deeper Than the Midterms

Elon Musk has enjoyed a cozy relationship with top Texas brass for years. And in recent weeks, as the midterm elections approach and Musk’s financial support of the Texas GOP has become virtually limitless, that relationship has gone under the microscope.

While polls suggest that a number of races in deep-red Texas are looking dizzyingly close, Federal Election Commission filings show that Musk has given at least $158 million to super PACs supporting Texas attorney general Ken Paxton’s bid for Senate, and last week Musk explicitly endorsed him in a post on X. “The fate of Texas and America is at stake,” Musk wrote. “Vote for @KenPaxtonTX today.”

Newly released state campaign filings also show that Musk also donated $5,000,000 to Governor Greg Abbott’s bid for reelection, making him his single largest donor.

Abbott’s relationship with Musk has been the subject of public interest for years. State representative Gina Hinojosa, who is running against Abbott, recently sued to view, in full, 1,400 pages of the governor’s correspondences with Musk. Abbott has been trying to block their release for some time; his office has described the communications as too “intimate and embarrassing” to be made public. This week, a judge ruled that Abbott had illegally “obstructed and continues to obstruct” Hinojosa’s right to inspect the documents in her capacity as a state lawmaker and ordered their release to her. Abbott has since appealed; a hearing is scheduled for November 2, one day before the election.

State representative James Talarico, who is running against Paxton for Senate, has campaigned on his opponents’ checkered past. As attorney general, Paxton has been indicted on felony securities fraud charges (which he settled without a plea), was accused by whistleblowers of using his office to benefit the financial interests of a political donor, and was impeached (though later acquitted).

And at a campaign event on Monday in El Paso, Talarico raised questions about Paxton and Musk’s relationship. “Ken Paxton has the ultimate megadonor,” Talarico said. “Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat.”

But Musk’s business dealings in Texas politics didn’t start with the midterms. For years, he has enjoyed lucrative state contacts, tax breaks, and allyship from Texas leaders. In 2021, Musk moved Tesla’s corporate headquarters from Palo Alto, California, to Austin, and SpaceX’s headquarters from Hawthorne, California, to Starbase, Texas, in 2024.

Musk’s initial relocation to Texas coincided with a shift in operations inside the Texas Attorney General’s office. In the past, lawyers would prepare notices of investigation (administrative subpoenas known as CIDs) based on public complaints or evidence collected, then send them up the chain for approval.

Sources tell WIRED that from about 2021 onward, lawyers were increasingly instructed by Texas’ executive branch—which included Paxton and Abbott—who and what they were going to investigate, despite internal efforts to steer resources toward more “legitimate” issues. For example, in 2022, eyebrows were raised internally when, the same day Musk sent a letter to Twitter threatening to abandon a $44 billion acquisition agreement over Twitter’s alleged misrepresentation of the number of bots on the platform, Paxton’s office issued a statement asserting that his office would be launching its own investigation against Twitter.

A year later, Paxton once again appeared to use his office to benefit Musk. Musk sued the progressive watchdog Media Matters for defamation after it published an investigation showing that X, under Musk’s ownership, had been placing ads from major brands next to white-nationalist content. Moments after he filed his suit, Paxton’s office announced its own investigation into Media Matters. (Media Matters sued Paxton, asserting that his investigation was brought out of retaliation for its coverage of Musk and X.) In 2024, after Musk filed an antitrust lawsuit against the World Federation of Advertisers and major brands, accusing them of a conspiracy to pull revenue from X, Paxton announced his own investigation into the organization, accusing them of a “potential anticompetitive scheme to withhold advertising dollars from certain social media platforms.” (He did not mention X by name.)

And when the Department of Justice’s Public Integrity Section wrote a letter to Musk warning that his America PAC million-dollar sweepstakes program ahead of the presidential election could violate federal election law, Paxton intervened by filing a FOIA request, accusing the government of “intimidation of businessman Elon Musk.”

This summer, Musk’s activities in Texas didn’t slow down: Texas legislators called for an audit after the Texas Broadband Development Office allocated $110 million in grants to Musk’s satellite internet company Starlink; Texas’ Office of the Comptroller recently announced that “Terafab,” Musk’s proposed 100-million-square-foot chip manufacturing facility in Grimes County, was the recipient of a $1.66 billion tax break; and SpaceX has also received around $30 million in state grants.

#553. Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease

A pesticide used for decades in agriculture may be linked to a much greater risk of Parkinson's disease, and scientists have uncovered a possible explanation for how it damages the brain.

Researchers at UCLA Health found that people with long-term residential exposure to chlorpyrifos, a widely used pesticide, had more than 2.5 times the risk of developing Parkinson's disease compared with those who were not exposed. Laboratory experiments also revealed how the chemical can interfere with the brain's ability to remove damaged proteins, leading to the loss of nerve cells essential for controlling movement.

The study, published in Molecular Neurodegeneration, goes beyond identifying a connection between pesticide exposure and Parkinson's. By examining what happens inside affected brain cells, the researchers uncovered a biological mechanism that could eventually provide new ways to protect the brain from damage.

A Common Pesticide With a Troubling Link to Parkinson's

Parkinson's disease affects nearly one million Americans. The progressive neurological condition gradually damages brain cells involved in movement, often causing tremors, muscle stiffness, slowed movement, and difficulties with coordination.

One of the defining features of Parkinson's is the loss of neurons that produce dopamine. This chemical messenger allows nerve cells to communicate and helps the brain coordinate smooth, controlled movements. As dopamine levels decline, the brain becomes less capable of regulating those movements.

Although inherited genetic factors can influence who develops Parkinson's, researchers have increasingly focused on environmental exposures that may also contribute to the disease. Pesticides are of particular interest because some chemicals used to kill insects or other agricultural pests can also interfere with biological processes in the nervous system.

Chlorpyrifos has been used extensively in agriculture for decades. Its residential use was banned in the United States in 2001, and agricultural applications faced additional restrictions in 2021. However, the pesticide remains in use on many crops in the United States and continues to be widely applied in other countries.

Because exposure may have occurred years before symptoms appeared, understanding the potential long-term effects of chlorpyrifos is particularly important. Identifying specific chemicals associated with Parkinson's could help researchers develop prevention strategies and determine whether previously exposed individuals might benefit from additional neurological monitoring.

Researchers Find More Than Double the Parkinson's Risk

To investigate the connection, UCLA scientists examined information from 829 people diagnosed with Parkinson's disease and 824 people without the condition. All participants were enrolled in the university's long-running Parkinson's Environment and Genes study, which investigates how environmental exposures and inherited factors influence Parkinson's risk.

The researchers combined California's detailed pesticide application records with participants' residential and workplace address histories. This allowed them to estimate how much chlorpyrifos individuals may have encountered over time based on where they lived and worked.

The results revealed a striking association. People with prolonged residential exposure to chlorpyrifos had more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease compared with those who had no such exposure.

Although this population analysis could not establish that the pesticide directly caused Parkinson's, the researchers took an additional step to investigate whether chlorpyrifos could produce the kinds of brain damage seen in people with the disease.

The team exposed mice to chlorpyrifos in aerosol form for 11 weeks. The inhalation approach was designed to resemble a common way people may encounter pesticides in the environment.

The exposed mice developed movement difficulties and lost neurons responsible for producing dopamine. This was particularly significant because the degeneration of these same nerve cells is a central feature of Parkinson's disease.

The researchers also detected inflammation in the animals' brains, along with abnormal accumulations of a protein called alpha-synuclein.

Under normal conditions, alpha-synuclein is found in nerve cells and plays a role in their functioning. However, the protein can accumulate in abnormal clumps that are closely associated with Parkinson's disease. These deposits are a major focus of research into why certain brain cells gradually deteriorate.

Together, the findings showed that chlorpyrifos exposure could reproduce several important characteristics of Parkinson's in laboratory animals, strengthening the biological evidence behind the human population findings.

Scientists Uncover a Breakdown in the Brain's Cleanup System

The researchers then turned to zebrafish to investigate exactly how chlorpyrifos harms neurons. These small fish are frequently used in neuroscience research because they allow scientists to study biological processes involved in nerve cell development and survival.

Their experiments pointed to a disruption in autophagy, a natural cellular maintenance process that helps remove damaged proteins and other unwanted material.

Autophagy functions much like an internal recycling system. Cells use it to break down worn-out or defective components so that potentially harmful material does not accumulate. This process is especially important for neurons, many of which must remain functional throughout a person's lifetime.

When chlorpyrifos interfered with this cleanup system, damaged material accumulated inside neurons, contributing to their deterioration.

The researchers also made an encouraging discovery. When they restored the cellular cleanup process or removed synuclein protein in their experiments, the neurons were protected from damage.

This finding suggests that the pesticide's harmful effects may depend partly on a biological pathway that researchers could potentially target with future treatments.

A Potential New Strategy for Protecting Against Parkinson's

The discovery raises the possibility of developing therapies that strengthen the brain's cellular cleanup mechanisms and help protect vulnerable neurons. Such treatments might eventually prove useful for people exposed to chlorpyrifos or other pesticides that disrupt similar processes.

However, the protective effects have so far been demonstrated in laboratory models. Additional research will be needed to determine whether enhancing autophagy can prevent or reduce pesticide-related brain damage in humans.

Scientists also want to investigate whether other commonly used pesticides interfere with the same cellular mechanisms. Although chlorpyrifos use has declined in the United States, many people were exposed before restrictions were introduced, and related agricultural chemicals remain widely used.

The findings could also help identify people with a history of substantial pesticide exposure who may benefit from closer neurological monitoring. Earlier recognition of possible changes in brain function could become increasingly important as researchers work toward treatments that slow or prevent Parkinson's progression.

Dr. Jeff Bronstein, professor of Neurology at UCLA Health and the study's senior author, emphasized the importance of identifying a particular chemical rather than treating all pesticides as a single category.

"This study establishes chlorpyrifos as a specific environmental risk factor for Parkinson's disease, not just pesticides as a general class," said Dr. Jeff Bronstein.

"By showing the biological mechanism in animal models, we've demonstrated that this association is likely causal. The discovery that autophagy dysfunction drives the neurotoxicity also points us toward potential therapeutic strategies to protect vulnerable brain cells."

#552. Anthropic takes steps to block Claude from reverse-engineering video games

According to reporting from Tom's Hardware, Anthropic's Claude AI has quietly started restricting the kinds of work it will do, including modding, decompiling, or reverse-engineering video game code. And though there has as yet been no official announcement about why, the reason is still pretty obvious.

The video game community has been in the news a lot lately, first because of the GTA6 leaks that went mega-viral and spurred Take-Two Interactive into getting subpoenas against both Microsoft and Discord in the hopes of finding the responsible parties, and next because the hacking and modding community discovered how much easier AI makes their job.

First, game decompilers went into overdrive, playing around with the source code of multiple different video games to, for example, put Nintendo's Mario inside the dark gothic world of Elden Ring, or import Spider-Man into the Batman: Arkham City game, seamlessly blending the mechanics of one character into the world of another. Next came the ports: World of Warcraft, Call of Duty, and Grand Theft Auto: Vice City made playable in a browser, without the original developers or copyright owners having any say in the matter.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

These initial modifications and ports were already giving gaming companies nightmares, teasing a future without system gatekeeping, but things really got out of hand with the PlayStation 5 jailbreak, which resulted in everything from backward compatibility with older-gen PlayStation games to cross-platform play, with users figuring out how to run Xbox-exclusive titles like Halo 2 and acclaimed Nintendo titles like Zelda: Breath of the Wild on a jailbroken PS5.

Given the potential number of lawsuits these jailbreaks could cause, and the astronomically high nature of the monetary damages, it's no surprise that AI companies are scrambling to shut down or severely restrict these pathways, but it's also deeply ironic. As Tom's Hardware reporter Bruno Ferreira notes, this sudden concern for copyright "highlights the irony of frontier AI companies that copied the world's information and art for their training sets and are now concerned with copyright infringement."

There's also the ugly truth that, if one company makes a gesture toward respecting copyright law or basic ethics, the bad actors can find another LLM that won't (or hasn't yet) taken the same precautions, creating a kind of AI arms race driven by perverse incentives: the least ethical AI might be poised to become the most popular.

#550. This App Brutally Shames You by Tracking How Many Hours You’ve Lost to Scrolling

You know that phone addiction has become a big issue when even Google and Apple are bundling time management tools into their handsets—Digital Wellbeing and Screen Time, respectively. There are now also a plethora of apps looking to help you cultivate a healthier relationship with your device.

One of the newer ones, which takes a slightly different approach to the norm, is Oh My Hours for iOS. (There's no sign of an Android version yet.) Rather than giving you a mass of menus and options to wade through, it simply splits each day into blocks of hours that you can either waste or use productively, then puts a black mark next to the hours during which your phone has distracted you.

It's simple, it's effective, and it just might work. Rather than seeing how long you spent on X and Instagram, you see the hours you've lost to social media algorithms and the infinite scroll. Here's how Oh My Hours works on your iPhone, plus some other apps to check out if you’re looking to develop healthier phone habits.

You can get started with Oh My Hours for free on iOS. But to really make the most of it, a $10-per-year or $20 lifetime payment is required. This lets you customize what counts as a “lost” hour or day, and it gives you access to month and year views, which provide the best insights into how you're spending time on your phone.

Here's how it works. First, you indicate which apps you consider distractions, either by category (social media apps and games, for example) or by selecting apps individually. If you use any distracting app for a certain amount of time—this can be customized in settings—then that hour of the day is marked as “lost.”

The main interface shows each day as a straightforward series of circles representing hours. Every circle that’s filled in black is an hour you’ve lost to an app that has pulled you away from something more worthwhile.

It’s quite a brutal and minimalist approach, but I like it. It really brings home how much time you can spend on apps that aren’t really all that good for you, especially when you start looking at your progress (or lack of it) over entire weeks or months. However, I did find that once I’d lost a particular hour, my brain wanted to cram in as much absent-minded scrolling as possible during the rest of that hour.

By default, an hour is marked as lost if only if you spend seconds inside a distracting app. It's quite a harsh approach, but it needs to be—otherwise I think there would be the temptation to use up any allotted free time after every hour resets. You can extend this threshold period through settings, if you pay for the app.

Another handy feature here is the ability to set designated quiet hours. These are times when you really, absolutely do not want to look at your phone unnecessarily: Any use of a distracting app here blackens the boxes for all the hours in the quiet zone, not just one. Again, this can be customized, whether or not you’re using the app for free.

There’s one more option here, which is to reset an hour if you think it’s been marked incorrectly. (Maybe your finger slipped and you really didn’t mean to launch Instagram.) It’s all very simple and easy to use, and there’s an export tool here that gives you a CSV file of your stats if you want to do more with them.

As I’ve already mentioned, if you’re in the market for an app that’ll gently nudge your habits toward spending less time on your phone, there are abundant options that look at the problem from a variety of angles. These are in addition to the Digital Wellbeing (Android) and Screen Time (iOS) tools you’ll find on your phone, which can be accessed from the Settings screens.

One Sec for Android or iOS takes a simple approach to phone addiction. For the apps you specify, it will load up a breathing exercise for you to complete before giving you the choice to continue to the app or back out. It’s a small tweak, but it’s surprisingly effective, and it’s backed by science. You can get started for free, while $20 a year gets you more features, including full app blocking and more advanced time tracking.

Then there’s Forest, for Android or iOS, which I’ve found to be useful whenever I’ve wanted to try to encourage myself to spend less time on my phone. The longer you ignore your handset, the bigger your virtual forest grows, and the app developers invest in real tree planting to further incentivize you. The main focus timer can be used without paying, while upgrades like customizations and allowed lists will set you back at least $6 a month.

ScreenZen, available for Android or iOS, is comprehensive and completely free (though you can donate to the developer if you find it helpful, which I’d recommend). You can set up a variety of barriers between you and your distracting apps, depending on your preference, including customized pauses (with motivational messages) and math challenges. Conventional app and timer blocks are also included.

One of the most thorough options here is Roots, though it’s available only on iOS. You’re able to schedule phone-free periods, block specific apps, and set up phone detox challenges that you can take on with friends and family. Like Oh My Hours, the app is also really good at giving you a breakdown of how much time you’ve saved by staying out of certain apps. Basic blocks and limits are free, with more advanced customizations available for $10 a month.

Also worth considering is Brick, which combines the free Android or iOS app with a small physical device that’ll set you back $59. The Brick itself is an NFC transmitter (it works like tap-to-pay), and when you want some distraction-free time, just press your phone against it to block (or unblock) specific apps. The controls are all managed in the Brick app. It’s incredibly simple, and that’s what makes it effective.

#549. 30,000-year-old DNA reveals Ice Age Europeans were far more connected than we thought

More than 30,000 years ago, people living across Ice Age Europe were far more connected than scientists previously believed. New genetic evidence reveals unexpected links between populations separated by enormous distances, challenging the long-held idea that eastern and western European groups remained largely isolated from one another.

An international research team led by the University of Vienna made the discovery by analyzing ancient DNA from rare human remains and traces of human genetic material preserved in cave sediments. Published in Science Advances, the findings provide a new picture of how prehistoric Europeans interacted, exchanged genes, and maintained populations through thousands of years of dramatic environmental change.

The research focuses on people associated with one of Europe's major Paleolithic cultures (the Gravettian), which flourished across the continent roughly 34,000 to 25,000 years ago. Archaeological discoveries have long suggested that these ancient populations maintained connections over considerable distances. However, previous genetic evidence pointed to relatively distinct eastern and western ancestry groups.

By combining new genetic findings with previously collected DNA, researchers uncovered evidence that these groups were more interconnected than expected. They also found signs that certain populations in southwestern Europe maintained their genetic ancestry for thousands of years.

A Woman From 30,000 Years Ago Reveals Hidden Genetic Connections

One of the most revealing discoveries came from the remains of a woman who lived approximately 30,000 years ago in what is now southwestern France. Found at Isturitz Cave, her remains provided the oldest genome-wide genetic dataset yet obtained from a modern human in southwestern Europe.

Her DNA contained a surprising combination of ancestry. Although most of her genetic background was associated with western European populations, she also carried ancestry linked to people from central and eastern Europe.

Using genetic modeling, researchers estimated that this mixing between populations occurred approximately 32,500 to 31,500 years ago. The finding suggests that genetic connections extended across large portions of Europe much earlier than scientists had previously established.

"Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed," says first author Pere Gelabert, Department of Evolutionary Anthropology at the University of Vienna. "Gene flow across such large distances adds a new dimension to our understanding of how Gravettian populations were connected."

The researchers identified a similar genetic signature in another ancient individual whose remains had previously been studied at Ormesson, France. Combined with archaeological discoveries, the evidence strengthens the possibility that Isturitz Cave served as a gathering place where different groups of prehistoric people encountered one another.

Ancient DNA Hidden in Cave Sediments Reveals Ice Age Survival

While some ancient Europeans exchanged genes across considerable distances, other populations appear to have maintained a continuous genetic presence in particular regions for thousands of years.

Evidence from Chufín Cave in northern Spain suggests that ancestry associated with western European populations persisted in southwestern Europe over an extended period.

The researchers also used an increasingly valuable technique that allows scientists to recover human DNA directly from cave sediments, even when no identifiable human remains are present. Tiny traces of genetic material left behind by ancient inhabitants can survive in soil and other deposits for thousands of years, providing information about people whose bones have never been found.

At El Mirón Cave in Cantabria, Spain, the team recovered human nuclear DNA from a sediment layer dating back approximately 22,000 years. Despite finding no human bones or teeth in the layer, they obtained enough genetic information to determine the ancestry of the people who had occupied the site.

"Sedimentary DNA allows us to recover genetic information from periods where human remains are missing," says senior author Ron Pinhasi, Department of Evolutionary Anthropology at the University of Vienna, whose team led this study. "This gives us a way to connect archaeological layers with the genetic ancestry of the people who occupied a site."

The results indicate that western European ancestry persisted in the region through the Last Glacial Maximum, a period when enormous ice sheets reached their greatest extent during the last Ice Age.

This supports the idea that the Iberian Peninsula, which includes present-day Spain and Portugal, served as an important refuge for prehistoric humans during some of the coldest conditions of the Ice Age.

Ancient Mother and Son Offer Clues About Prehistoric Mating

Another revealing discovery came from southern Italy, where researchers examined the genetic remains of Ostuni1b, a male fetus believed to be the son of a previously studied woman known as Ostuni1.

Genetic analysis suggests that the child's father likely belonged to the same ancestral population as his mother. However, the parents were not closely related, offering evidence that mating patterns within these ancient communities may have helped limit inbreeding.

This finding adds another dimension to the emerging picture of prehistoric European societies. Even as some populations maintained relatively stable genetic ancestry within their home regions, they could also participate in broader networks of genetic exchange spanning considerable distances.

Together, the discoveries show that long-term regional continuity and widespread genetic connections were not mutually exclusive. Both helped shape the population history of Ice Age Europe.

Building on these results, Gelabert and his colleagues are now combining DNA recovered from ancient sediments with advanced proteomic techniques, which examine proteins for clues about past life. Their goal is to investigate the earliest expansions of modern humans across Europe, including how these populations interacted with carnivores in places where bones and other organic remains are scarce.

#548. Majority of teens and tweens now use chat bots, new research finds

An alarming new survey from media and tech non-profit Common Sense Media has found that children begin interacting with AI chatbots at an alarmingly early age — with nearly half of 9-12-year-olds having bypassed the 13+ age restriction common to most LLMs.

The survey is titled The 2026 Common Sense Media Census: Tech and Media Use by Tweens and Teens. In the paper, the organization conducted interviews with more than 1,200 American children aged 9 to 17, asking questions about AI use as well as television, gaming, and social media habits. More importantly, the interviews asked these young children how they feel about their own media consumption habits.

Standout findings include the sharp rise in smartphone ownership, with more than half of 11-year-olds already owning a smartphone and near-universal smartphone access by age 17, as well as the incredible amount of time spent on screens: eight hours per day for teenagers and five hours per day for tweens.

Because social scientists were caught unprepared by the massive impact social media has had on teen mental health, there's a strong push for more studies into the effects of AI interaction on teenagers, especially in the areas of school preparedness and mental health.

A second study, titled "Exploring Artificial Intelligence [AI]: Understanding Relationships between AI Use and Mental Health Among Middle and High School Students," was commissioned by the JEF Foundation, a mental health advocacy group. They interviewed more than 5,000 American middle and high school students from 21 different schools between Oct. 2025 and April 2026, which resulted in the following four findings, taken verbatim from their report:

Students use AI for a wide range of cognitive and emotional support, including turning to AI when they’re struggling emotionally.

Certain uses of AI are associated with worse mental health and well-being outcomes, and greater lifetime history of suicidal thoughts and attempts.

Students who use AI while emotionally struggling have worse mental health and well-being outcomes, and greater history of suicidal thoughts and attempts.

Patterns of AI use differ across demographics, with important implications for mental health disparities.

JED Foundation psychologist Kayla Anderson summarized the findings to NPR: "When young people are using AI, when they're in emotional distress, they're more likely to report poor mental health and well-being outcomes," but she was also quick to stress that the study did not establish causality. In other words, they don't know if AI is making teen mental health worse, or if teens with worse mental health are gravitating to AI chatbots for help.

Thankfully, there are already a slew of new studies set to conclude soon investigating whether causality can be established. If so, expect lawmakers to come down hard on AI companies to impose more stringent age restrictions and accept greater liability for poor mental health outcomes among teenagers.

#546. Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists

Scientists have proposed a surprising new explanation for why the universe exists, and it centers on a mysterious particle that physicists have largely overlooked for decades. Their theory suggests this forgotten particle may have played a crucial role in shaping the early cosmos and allowing matter to survive after the Big Bang.

The research addresses one of the most fundamental mysteries in physics: why does the universe contain matter instead of nothing at all? Scientists believe matter and antimatter were produced in nearly equal amounts in the early universe. When these opposites encounter one another, they annihilate and release energy. If they had existed in perfectly equal quantities, virtually all matter could have disappeared, leaving no material to form stars, planets, or life.

Now, researchers from the University of Southampton and the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur believe they may have found an important piece of the puzzle. Their explanation involves a little-understood relative of the neutrino, an extremely lightweight particle that rarely interacts with ordinary matter.

A Forgotten Particle With a Powerful Role in the Early Universe

The team focused on a type of particle known as a 'decoupled' heavy neutrino. Unlike ordinary neutrinos, this hypothetical heavier relative has generally been considered too weakly connected to other particles to significantly influence the universe.

However, the researchers found that its unusually long lifetime could have made it far more important than previously thought. According to their calculations, the particle may have survived long enough to temporarily dominate the universe's energy density as the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang.

That brief period of dominance could have altered how the early universe evolved, influencing the conditions that ultimately allowed matter to outnumber antimatter.

Dr. Rishav Roshan of the University of Southampton, an author of the study, explained:

"This decoupled heavy neutrino has long been dismissed as an irrelevant background detail in particle physics.

"However, it decays incredibly slowly. As the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang, the particle lived long enough that it temporarily took over the energy density of the universe and triggered a matter-dominated period."

The findings were published in Physical Review Letters, a scientific journal of the American Physical Society.

How a Heavy Neutrino Could Explain Why Matter Survived

Previous attempts to explain why matter prevailed over antimatter generally left out the decoupled heavy neutrino. Because it interacts so weakly with other particles, scientists assumed it would have little influence on the processes responsible for creating the imbalance.

The new research challenges that assumption. The team found that even a particle with extremely weak interactions could indirectly affect the conditions under which matter gained its crucial advantage.

This imbalance, known as matter and antimatter asymmetry, is essential to understanding our existence. For reasons physicists are still trying to explain, the early universe ended up with slightly more matter than antimatter. That small difference allowed some matter to remain after most particles and their antiparticles annihilated one another.

"The fact that we are here at all proves that an asymmetry between matter and antimatter occurred," added Dr. Roshan.

"The decoupled neutrino shifted the temperature in the early universe at which fundamental particles - like electrons and other leptons - interacted with their anti-particles with the help of Standard Model Higgs boson.

"This temperature acts like a switch that shapes how the matter-antimatter imbalance was built up."

The Higgs boson is a fundamental particle associated with the mechanism that gives many elementary particles their mass. In the researchers' proposed scenario, the heavy neutrino changed the temperature conditions governing important particle interactions involving the Higgs boson.

By shifting when these interactions occurred, the particle could have influenced how the imbalance between matter and antimatter developed. In other words, something long considered insignificant may have helped determine why the universe contains matter at all.

Ancient Gravitational Waves Could Reveal the Answer

The theory could also have important implications for understanding how the universe expanded in its earliest stages.

Study co-author Dr. Sudipta Show of the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur said the findings suggest that the forgotten particle may have dramatically altered the expansion history of the young cosmos.

He added: "It offers us a new explanation for how matter won.

"The dramatic shift in the early expansion of the cosmos leaves distinct but detectable imprints of changes, for example on primordial gravitational waves.

"These gravitational wave signatures open up new avenues for us to unravel the evolution of the early universe after the Big Bang."

Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of space and time. Scientists believe processes in the extremely early universe may have generated primordial gravitational waves that carry information about conditions from that distant era.

According to the new theory, the temporary dominance of the heavy neutrino could have left recognizable signatures in those ancient signals. Detecting such patterns could eventually provide a way to investigate whether the proposed particle really influenced the universe's earliest evolution.

For now, the explanation remains theoretical. But it offers physicists a new possibility for solving one of cosmology's deepest mysteries: how matter survived when its encounter with antimatter could have left the universe almost entirely empty.

#545. The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Was Pulled Off in Just 20 Minutes

Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.

Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however.

Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.”

The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis. “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations.

“Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains.

The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor. Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity.

Neither Binance nor law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector, but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks.

Within North Korea’s sprawling hacking operations—often designed to earn money for the highly sanctioned and repressive regime—TraderTraitor has stood out in recent years for its sophistication and targeting of crypto and decentralized finance companies. Last year, the FBI named TraderTraitor as being responsible for the $1.5 billion hack against crypto exchange Bybit.

Binance did not answer WIRED’s questions about whether it believes North Korean hackers are behind the colossal heist, pointing towards a statement saying it will cover all losses from the hack and is working with law enforcement officials to identify who is responsible.

“Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” the company says in a statement. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it.”

“These folks in particular are somewhat artists in terms of getting into these distributed finance organizations,” Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “TraderTraitor seems to focus on these larger operations. In the past, they’ve developed their own fake applications and tried to use those to get inside organizations.”

TRM and Chainalysis have initially linked the attack to TraderTraitor and say the determinations are based on their analysis of both on-chain and off-chain activity. “​​The strongest evidence emerged when Chainalysis investigators observed, in real time, funds stolen from Binance commingling with funds stolen in last month’s Bitget exploit, which had been attributed to North Korean actors,” a research blog from Chainalysis says.

“Binance says the attack began with a compromised engineer’s laptop. Targeting crypto company staff is a TraderTraitor hallmark,” Elliptic’s Robinson says. “The attacker funded their wallet through Tornado Cash and rehearsed the attack in advance, as in Bybit.”

While around $3 billion of cryptocurrency was initially frozen in the aftermath of the attack, it is likely those behind it could still potentially take away huge sums as not all of the stolen crypto can be frozen. Research from Chainalysis says the company is seeing money “laundering patterns we have not seen before” and that thousands of transactions being quickly processed indicates that they are using “automation to obscure the trail of funds.”

Elliptic’s Robinson says that around $2.8 billion, or around 44 percent of the total amount stolen, has been frozen by crypto companies and exchanges so far, with almost all of this being stablecoins. “The remaining $3.3 billion is mostly Bitcoin, Ether, and XRP, which no one can freeze,” Robinson says. “It can only be stopped when it reaches an exchange or other service. Some will be caught over the coming months, but I don’t expect the frozen share to rise much further.”

#544. Merck tops quarterly estimates, hikes profit outlook as new Keytruda form shows strength

Merck on Thursday topped third-quarter estimates and hiked its adjusted profit outlook, as its immunotherapy Keytruda, including a newer injectable form of the drug, showed stronger-than-expected sales.

The pharmaceutical giant now expects adjusted earnings to be between $2.77 and $2.82 per share. That adjusted profit outlook is up from a previous range of $2.66 to $2.76 per share. The guidance now includes a one-time charge of $400 million, or 12 cents per share, related to its licensing agreement with the Chinese cancer drugmaker SciBrunch.

Merck also narrowed the low end of its 2026 revenue guidance, now expecting sales between $66.8 billion and $67.3 billion. That compares to a previous outlook of $66.3 billion to $67.3 billion.

The company has been on a deal spree as it races to offset generic competition for Keytruda after key patents begin expiring in 2028.

Merck is also positioning the new form of the drug, Keytruda Qlex, as a cornerstone of its growth strategy. The goal is to transition patients from the original intravenous version to Qlex, considered a more convenient under-the-skin injection. This strategy allows the company to defend its market share and sustain Keytruda's blockbuster sales beyond the original version's loss of exclusivity.

Keytruda raked in $8.60 billion in sales for the quarter, beating the $7.73 billion that analysts were expecting, according to StreetAccount. That includes $830 million in sales for Qlex – the highest seen in a quarter since it launched in 2025.

Analysts were expecting $649 million in sales, StreetAccount estimates said. The blowout quarter for the shot suggests it could soon eventually be a multibillion-dollar product annually.

Here's what Merck reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

The company posted a net income of $5.07 billion, or $2.04 per share, for the quarter. That compares with net income of $5.79 billion, or $2.32 per share, for the year-earlier period.

Excluding acquisition and restructuring costs, Merck posted earnings of $2.49 per share for the third quarter.

Merck raked in $18.09 billion in revenue for the quarter, up 5% from the same period a year earlier.

Beyond Keytruda, Merck's newer products also showed strong growth.

Winrevair, which is used to treat a rare, deadly lung condition, generated $694 million in sales for the quarter, up 93% from the same period a year earlier. Analysts were expecting sales of $645 million.

Meanwhile, the Gardasil vaccine, which prevents cancers from HPV, a very common sexually transmitted infection, drew about $2 billion in sales due to higher demand in the U.S. That tops the $1.76 billion in sales that analysts were expecting.

That strong revenue comes after Merck last year grappled with elevated Gardasil inventory and weak demand for the vaccine in China.

Meanwhile, Merck's animal health business posted $1.68 billion in sales for the third quarter, which came in slightly below analysts' estimates.

#542. NASA's Hubble and Webb discover ancient worlds that remember their past

NASA's Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have uncovered surprising clues about the earliest days of our solar system by examining some of the smallest and faintest objects ever observed beyond Neptune. The findings challenge expectations about how planets form and suggest that these distant, icy bodies have preserved evidence of their origins for billions of years.

For the first time, astronomers combined observations from Hubble and Webb to investigate trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs), tiny bodies that travel around the Sun far beyond Neptune's orbit. Researchers discovered 27 previously unknown objects, but their findings revealed an unexpected puzzle. There were fewer small objects than some theories predicted, and their colors closely resembled those of much larger objects in the same distant regions.

These frozen remnants offer a rare opportunity to study the materials that eventually became planets. Most are extraordinarily difficult to detect, shining more than 100 million times more faintly than objects visible to the naked eye. Two related studies published in The Astronomical Journal examined the newly identified objects to learn more about their sizes, compositions, and ancient history.

Ancient Building Blocks of the Solar System

Scientists believe planets began forming when tiny particles of dust and pebbles orbiting the young Sun gradually accumulated into larger bodies. Over time, these materials formed objects roughly the size of cities, known as "planetesimals." These early building blocks eventually combined to create the planets we see today.

However, that final stage of growth did not occur for many objects beyond Neptune. Instead of developing into full-sized planets, countless smaller bodies remained, preserving evidence of the solar system's earliest period of formation.

To investigate these distant survivors, research teams led by PhD candidates at the University of Victoria in Canada, working under the guidance of the National Research Council of Canada, and Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff conducted the deepest survey of trans-Neptunian objects to date. Both space telescopes observed the same region of sky simultaneously, with Hubble collecting visible light and Webb capturing infrared light.

By combining these observations, astronomers could examine the objects' colors, estimate their sizes, and determine how they orbit the Sun. Their colors are especially valuable because they provide clues about the chemical makeup of their surfaces, much like fingerprints that reveal an object's identity and history.

The researchers focused on two distinct populations of trans-Neptunian objects, known as dynamically "cold" and dynamically "hot" TNOs. These descriptions refer to their orbital behavior rather than their temperatures.

Cold objects have largely remained in the regions where they originally formed. They follow relatively circular paths around the Sun and stay close to the plane in which most of the solar system's planets orbit.

Hot objects have experienced a much more turbulent history. They originally formed between the present-day orbits of Uranus and Neptune but were scattered outward as the giant planets shifted positions early in the solar system's development. Their current orbits are much more elongated, and they travel above and below the solar system's main orbital plane.

Despite these dramatically different histories, the two populations revealed an unexpected similarity. Even the smallest objects appear to have retained surface characteristics resembling those of their larger counterparts.

Tiny Worlds Preserve Their Ancient Origins

Before the observations, scientists suspected that smaller TNOs would show clear evidence of repeated collisions over billions of years. Impacts could have fractured the objects and exposed fresh material, potentially changing their surface compositions and colors.

Instead, the newly discovered objects displayed the same general color relationships seen among larger TNOs. This suggests that collisions may have altered their surfaces much less than expected.

One possibility is that these objects have experienced fewer impacts than astronomers previously assumed. Another is that their surfaces somehow retain their original compositions even after collisions. Researchers have not yet determined which explanation is correct.

"You could imagine a scenario where getting knocked around and fragmented would change the surface composition, and then you would see a different surface color for tiny TNOs compared to their larger siblings. So it's really fascinating to see that the smallest objects are somehow 'remembering' and preserving the history of how they were made," said Northern Arizona University PhD candidate Anastasia Morgan, who led the study of color and composition.

"These dynamically 'hot' TNOs retain a signature of where they were born, even though they've been orbitally scrambled since then," said co-author David Trilling of Northern Arizona University.

The observations indicate that both hot and cold TNOs have maintained color patterns linked to their formation, with surprisingly little apparent change since the solar system's beginnings. These ancient objects may therefore preserve important information about the environments in which they first took shape.

Webb Finds Fewer Tiny Worlds Than Expected

The James Webb Space Telescope also provided another important piece of the puzzle. Its observations allowed scientists to examine how many objects exist at different sizes, revealing an unexpected resemblance between the two populations.

Although hot and cold TNOs formed in different parts of the early solar system, their overall size distributions were remarkably alike. This suggests that the processes responsible for creating planetesimals may have operated in much the same way across different environments.

"It's very interesting that the process of planetesimal formation ends up producing the same distribution of sizes for both cold and hot populations, despite forming in different regions of the early solar system. The process seems to be insensitive to disk conditions, producing similar planetesimal sizes whether the disk is hot or cold, and dense or fluffy," said University of Victoria PhD candidate Marielle Eduardo, who led the study on size distribution.

The researchers also identified a surprising shortage of very small TNOs compared with predictions from some existing planet formation models. Understanding why fewer objects were detected could help scientists refine their explanations of how the solar system's original building blocks developed.

Webb's extraordinary sensitivity made it possible to discover 27 exceptionally faint objects. One was so dim that detecting it would be comparable to standing on Earth and spotting a small swarm of fireflies on the Moon.

The smallest object measured just 3 miles (5 kilometers) across, making it approximately five times smaller than the objects detectable with even the most sensitive telescopes on the ground.

Hubble and Webb Reveal New Clues to Planet Formation

These discoveries depended on the complementary capabilities of NASA's two powerful space observatories. Hubble's ability to detect visible light and Webb's sensitivity to infrared light gave scientists a more complete picture of the distant objects than either telescope could have provided independently.

Together, the telescopes have opened a new window into a largely unexplored population of ancient solar system remnants. Their surprising similarities, preserved surface characteristics, and unexpected numbers offer important clues about the processes that shaped the planets billions of years ago.
